Each time, it is God who communicates something important to a person for their salvation or obedience. 3. The word can also mean to be instructed or taught by God in spiritual matters, as Moses received instructions for the tabernacle (Hebrews 8:5). 4. In a more general sense, the word can refer to the act of receiving a name or qualification: the disciples "were called Christians" in Antioch (Acts 11:26), which means they were given this name.
G5537.origine: The word comes from the Greek root "chrêma" (thing, good, matter), from which also comes the primitive meaning of "to transact, to consult." In the Greek scriptures of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "dabar" (word) when it concerns a word from God. The verb has specialized to designate divine communications: responses from oracles, then messages from God in the Bible. It is a word that has evolved from the concrete (to deal with a matter, to consult) to the divine (to receive a word from God).
G5537.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts, always to describe a communication from God to humans. In Matthew and Luke, it appears in the passive voice ("to be warned") and concerns revelations in dreams: to the wise men (Matthew 2:12), to Joseph (Matthew 2:22), to Simeon (Luke 2:26). In Acts, it describes the warning received by Cornelius via an angel (Acts 10:22) or the fact that a name has been given (Acts 11:26). In Hebrews, it designates the divine instruction received by Moses (Hebrews 8:5) and by Noah (Hebrews 11:7). The main meaning is always: to receive a message or direction that comes directly from God or his authority.
G5537.portee: This word reminds Christians that God communicates directly with his people, not through ordinary human means but through supernatural revelations (dreams, visions, angels, Holy Spirit). It assures that those who fear God and obey him can rely on his warnings and instructions to guide their decisions. It is a word of confidence: God does not leave his people without guidance when it is necessary for salvation or obedience.

sens: Word or message that God addresses directly to someone
Oracle, official announcement of God's will
G5538.detail:
1. The word designates a response that God gives to one who questions or listens — not just a simple thought, but a spoken word, a personal and direct message. In Romans 11:4, Paul asks: "But what is the divine response to him?" and then quotes the word that God addressed to the prophet Elijah: "I have reserved for myself seven thousand men…" It is the voice of God intervening in history and speaking to his servant.
2. More broadly, it is an oracle, that is, a solemn announcement of God's will or purpose. The word evokes the idea of an official proclamation, as when an authority communicates its decision. Here, God manifests himself through his word to remind Elijah that he has not abandoned his people.
G5538.origine: The word comes from the verb "chrématizô" which means "to deliver an official message, to convey a public word." It is related to "chrêma" (the thing, the matter) and to "chraomai" (to use, to consult). In common Greek, this verb was used to speak of an official response, an authorized opinion, or an oracle consultation. The Bible uses it to describe the words that God communicates directly to his servants.
G5538.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:4, where Paul uses it to quote the response that God gave to the prophet Elijah during his crisis of discouragement. Paul refers to the Old Testament (1 Kings 19:18) to show that God has never abandoned his faithful remnant in Israel. The context is that of a prophetic call: God responds to one who prays and seeks him.
G5538.portee: This word reminds us that God is not silent, but speaks to his people and addresses them with direct messages. For the believer, this means that God communicates his will and promises explicitly, notably through his written Word and his Spirit. It is an assurance that God listens and responds, even in times of doubt or solitude.

sens: That which can serve a purpose, which is advantageous or beneficial
That which produces a good effect, which brings profit or aid
That which is suitable for a given objective
G5539.detail:
1. The word describes what can serve, what has a concrete or moral utility. In 2 Timothy 2:14, Paul says that word disputes "only serve to ruin" — he speaks of a negative utility, a false utility that actually destroys: this shows that "useful" here means "capable of producing an effect," whether good or bad.
2. More broadly, the word evokes what is beneficial, what brings profit or advantage. Something useful is what we need, what helps us achieve a goal or progress in a direction.
3. In the Pauline ecclesial context, the useful stands in opposition to the sterile or harmful: what "serves" to build up faith is useful; what only divides or satisfies pride is not.
G5539.origine: The word comes from the verb "chraomai" (χράομαι), which means "to make use of, employ, serve." The adjective "useful" thus expresses the quality of what can be employed or put to profit. In ancient Greek, words from this family revolve around the practical idea of use and service: what is chrēsimos is by nature intended to serve, to be used for a good effect.
G5539.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:14. Paul exhorts Timothy to remind Christians to avoid word disputes "that only serve to ruin." The pastoral context is crucial: Paul does not condemn theological discussion itself, but sterile quarrels that, far from building up, destroy. The adjective "useful" thus raises the question: what is the real purpose of this word? Does it produce edification or division? This Pauline usage reveals that utility, in the Church, must always be measured against the standard of faith and charity.
G5539.portee: This word invites the Christian to ask the question of the real utility of their words and actions within the faith community. What seems useful at a moment (winning an argument, imposing one's viewpoint) can actually ruin others. The Pauline call pushes us to seek a deeper utility: that which builds up, unites, and leads to maturity in Christ. It is a call to wisdom and responsibility in our speech.

sens: Practical utilization of something, its function or usual employment
Habit, common way of doing or living
In a relational context, the normal and natural use of a person's body
G5540.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete use of something, what it is intended for or how it is used in daily life. It is the simple idea of use, of an ordinary function (Romans 1:26 speaks of "natural use").
2. By extension, it refers to a habit, an established practice, a recognized and accepted way of doing things — what everyone considers normal and appropriate (Romans 1:27 again contrasts this "natural use" with behavior that deviates from it).
3. In both verses from Romans, Paul uses "use" to describe the natural relationship between man and woman, as it was created and instituted. Here, the word takes on a very concrete and bodily sense: it is the normal and natural use of sexuality according to the order established by God.
G5540.origine: The word χρῆσις comes from the verb χράομαι, which means "to make use of," "to utilize." The root evokes the idea of using something, putting it into practice. It is a common word in Greek to simply denote the employment or use of something. In Hebrew, the Lord used the verb לִשְׁאוֹל ("to ask"), but these are two very different realities: χρῆσις truly conveys the idea of "practicing" or "using."
G5540.emploi: The word χρῆσις appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the passage of Romans 1:26-27, where Paul addresses the abandonment of natural relationships. In these two verses, Paul specifically uses this term to qualify the man-woman relationship as the "natural use," that is, the created and appropriate employment. When he mentions those who "abandon the natural use," he describes a deliberate deviation from what is established and natural. The word emphasizes normality, the created order, and the transgression that consists of turning away from it.
G5540.portee: This word reminds us that human sexuality is not a neutral or purely personal domain: it is inscribed within a created and natural order that God has established. Understanding "natural use" helps the reader grasp the ethical and theological stakes of the passage: it is not merely a preference, but a deviation from the function and purpose inscribed in creation itself.

sens: To show kindness to someone
To demonstrate gentleness and meekness in relationships
To act with generous and selfless kindness
G5541.detail:
1. To be kind means to show active goodness toward someone — it is less an inner disposition than a concrete behavior: to show gentleness, meekness, to treat others with kindness. In 1 Corinthians 13:4, Paul says that love "is full of kindness": it does not merely wish well, it expresses it through acts and words full of gentleness.
2. This verb evokes a generous and constant kindness, which strives to preserve peace and not to hurt. It stands in opposition to harshness, arrogance, impatience — all things that Paul enumerates just after to show what love is not.
G5541.origine: The verb comes from the Greek adjective χρηστός (chrēstos), which means "good, useful, easy to bear." This adjective first evokes what is pleasant, accommodating, non-oppressive. The root refers to the idea of what "fits well" or "is helpful." It is a rare word in biblical Greek: it appears only once, underscoring the importance of this trait in Paul's description of Christian love.
G5541.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Corinthians 13:4, at the heart of the hymn to love. Paul enumerates the qualities of Christian love in contrast to its opposite vices: love is patient (it endures), it is filled with kindness (it acts gently), it does not envy, does not boast, is not proud. The context shows that kindness is a visible and affective manifestation of love, a positive act of goodness toward others, not just a hidden intention.
G5541.portee: Kindness is one of the distinctive marks of true Christian love: it is that love which does not keep its qualities to itself, but actively deploys them for the good of others. It invites the believer to seek, in their daily words and actions, a generous gentleness that reflects Christ's goodness toward us.

sens: Gentle, pleasant, and flattering language
Deceptive speech using the sweetness of words to deceive
Deceptive eloquence intended to seduce
G5542.detail:
1. The word literally refers to a sweet word, a way of speaking that is pleasant to the ear. It is polite language, with kind words. In Romans 16:18, Paul speaks of sweet and flattering words that false preachers use.
2. These sweet words are not innocent: they aim to seduce and deceive. It is a discourse that pleases the ears but hides a malicious intent. The example in Romans 16:18 shows men who, through this deceptive eloquence, "seduce the hearts of the simple" — those who do not discern the cunning hidden beneath the kindness of the words.
3. The context shows that this sweet language serves to divert believers from Christ to the personal interests of the seducers. It is a weapon of manipulation: one dulls vigilance through the sweetness of tone.
G5542.origine: The Greek word χρηστολογία is formed from χρηστός (chrestos, "good, useful, kind") and λέγω (legô, "to speak"). Literally: "to speak with kindness." The same root χρηστός also gives us "Christian" (Χριστιανός) in the original sense of "disciple of Christ." But here, the compound χρηστολογία describes a discourse that has the appearance of goodness without having its substance — a beautiful facade for a hidden intention.
G5542.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Romans 16:18. Paul warns the Church in Rome against false preachers who have only one goal: to serve their own interest ("their own belly") instead of serving Christ. He shows that these seducers use sweet words as an instrument of deception. It is a pastoral warning: even the sweetest and most flattering words must be judged in the light of the truth of Christ and the fruit they produce in the heart.
G5542.portee: This word reminds the believer of an essential vigilance: the sweetness of words is not a guarantee of truth. A discourse can be pleasant and seductive while leading away from Christ. It is a call not to be lulled by eloquence, but to test every teaching against the measure of the Word of God and what truly edifies the Body of Christ.

sens: Pleasant to the taste or senses, easy to bear
Useful, suitable, fulfilling its function well
Of a kind character, generous, tender towards others
Morally right, virtuous
Characteristic of God: His mercy, kindness towards His creatures
G5543.detail:
1. This word primarily describes what pleases the senses or soothes: old wine is "good" because it has flavor (Luke 5:39), the yoke of Christ is "easy" because it does not weigh heavily on the one who bears it (Matthew 11:30). The image is that of something pleasant to experience.
2. It is also what works well, that is suitable for its use. "Good" morals (1 Corinthians 15:33) are virtuous habits that build an orderly life.
3. Applied to people, the word expresses kindness and tenderness: "Be kind to one another" (Ephesians 4:32) means to show compassion and forgiveness.
4. The word also falls under the moral register: it qualifies what is just and virtuous, in accordance with God's justice.
5. Finally, and most importantly, it characterizes the divine nature. God is "good" to the ungrateful and the wicked (Luke 6:35); His "goodness" leads to repentance (Romans 2:4). It is His merciful disposition towards humanity, not earned but freely given.
G5543.origine: The word comes from the verb χράομαι (to use, to make use of), hence the primary meaning: what is useful, practical, applicable. It has gradually come to designate what is pleasant or appropriate, and then what is morally good. In ancient Greek, it opposes what is sour, unpleasant, or harmful. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it most often translates the Hebrew word טוֹב (tov), the goodness and kindness of God towards Israel.
G5543.emploi: This word appears seven times in the New Testament. Three times it describes pleasant or appropriate things: wine, the yoke of Christ, morals. Four times it qualifies the goodness of a person or of God. In Paul (Romans 2:4, 1 Corinthians 15:33, Ephesians 4:32), it emphasizes the kindness of the believer towards others and the divine mercy that calls for conversion. In Luke and Peter, it exalts the kindness of Jesus and God. The context shows that it is never a weak or soft goodness, but an active and generous goodness.
G5543.portee: This word invites the Christian to discover God not only as powerful or just, but as good, merciful, and attractive. The "goodness of God" that "leads to repentance" shows that conversion does not arise from fear, but from the attraction exerted by divine love. For the believer, being "good" towards others means imitating this divine nature, thus becoming a reflection of Christ in the world.

sens: Moral excellence, righteousness
Kindness of heart, generosity towards others
Virtue produced by the Holy Spirit in the believer
G5544.detail:
1. Goodness is primarily a moral excellence, a rectitude of character: it is "doing good" in the most fundamental sense (Romans 3:12). It is the opposite of evil and sin.
2. Goodness especially denotes the active kindness of the heart, this disposition to do good to others, to show generosity and mercy. It is the goodness of God that leads us to repentance (Romans 2:4), and it is also that which God wants to show us in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:7). It is a force that acts, not just a feeling.
3. Goodness is a moral virtue that the Holy Spirit produces in the believer, alongside love, joy, and peace (Galatians 5:22). It characterizes the spiritual clothing of the Christian, along with mercy and gentleness (Colossians 3:12).
G5544.origine: The word comes from the adjective "chréstos" (useful, good, kind) and belongs to the same family as the Hebrew word "tov" (good, well), very common in the Greek Old Testament. The root evokes the idea of what is profitable, useful, that serves someone well — hence the meaning of "kindness": it is the goodness that benefits the one who receives it.
G5544.emploi: Goodness appears 8 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's letters. It first describes an absolute moral quality — the total absence of goodness characterizes sinful humanity (Romans 3:12). But it mainly designates the Christian virtue that God cultivates in the believer: it is part of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), alongside similar virtues such as benignity and gentleness. Paul contrasts it with God's severity (Romans 11:22) to show the two sides of His judgment: His goodness towards those who persevere, His severity towards those who fall. In Paul, God's goodness towards us is a call to repentance (Romans 2:4) and a reason for praise.
G5544.portee: Goodness reminds us that God is not only just — He is merciful and kind. His goodness is not passive: it drives us to change our lives and turn to Him. For the Christian, this word invites us to cultivate true goodness towards others, not just a simple respect for rules, but a generosity of heart that resembles that of God. It is the fruit of the Spirit, not a personal effort.

sens: the action of pouring holy oil on someone
the oil itself used for this action
the gift of the Holy Spirit that consecrates and transforms the believer
G5545.detail: 1. In the Old Testament, anointing involved pouring holy oil on the head of a person — kings, priests, prophets — to consecrate them to God and confer His power upon them. It was a visible and solemn ritual gesture that marked the beginning of their office. 2. The word also refers to the oil itself, this precious substance used in worship. This oil was not ordinary: it was prepared according to a special recipe and imbued every gesture with meaning. 3. In the letters of John, anointing takes on a spiritual meaning: it represents the gift of the Holy Spirit received by each believer at the moment of conversion. In 1 John 2:20 and 2:27, John speaks of the anointing as a living presence that remains in the heart of the disciple and guides them in the knowledge of God. This anointing teaches, guides, and protects against error.
G5545.origine: The Greek word chrisma comes from the verb chriô (to anoint). In Hebrew, the words mishkha (anointing) and associated variations express this same sacred action. The word is related to "Messiah" or "Christ," which literally means "the anointed one": it is therefore a word loaded with dignity and divine power.
G5545.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the first letter of John (2:20 and 2:27), addressed to disciples threatened by false teachers. John emphasizes that authentic believers have received an anointing from the Holy One, that is, a consecration and illumination by the Spirit. This anointing remains in them, teaches them all things, and preserves them from error. The anointing is not a one-time experience, but a lasting presence that guides the disciple in truth.
G5545.portee: For the believer, understanding the anointing reminds us that faith is not merely a mental assent or external obedience: it is an inner transformation marked by the presence of the Holy Spirit. Every Christian has been anointed by God Himself. This truth frees us from fear of false teachings and grants assurance: the Spirit dwells in us to guide us toward the truth. It is a source of confidence and spiritual freedom.

sens: one who follows Jesus Christ and believes in Him
one who bears the name of Christ
member of the community of Christ's disciples
G5546.detail:
1. A Christian is a person who believes in Jesus Christ and follows Him as Savior and Lord. It is someone who has placed their trust in Him for salvation.
2. The word "Christian" literally means "one who belongs to Christ" or "one who bears the name of Christ." In Antioch, the pagans gave this name to the disciples of Jesus to designate those who followed Jesus, called the Christ (Acts 11:26).
3. A Christian is a member of the community of believers, the Church, gathered around Jesus Christ. This name has marked from the beginning a new and distinct identity.
G5546.origine: The Greek word Χριστιανός is derived from Χριστός (Christos, "the Christ" or "the anointed one"), which comes from the Hebrew Messiah. The suffix -ανος (-anos) is a name-forming suffix that expresses belonging or adherence to someone or something. Thus, a Christian is literally "one who follows Christ" or "one of the party of Christ." This term originated in the Greco-Roman world to designate the new disciples of the Savior.
G5546.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in significant contexts. In Antioch, around the year 40, the pagans first gave the name "Christians" to the disciples of Jesus (Acts 11:26), thus marking the birth of the term. King Agrippa uses it ironically before Paul: "You persuade me to be a Christian" (Acts 26:28), showing the impact of apostolic testimony. Peter, on the other hand, wears this name with pride and defiance: if one suffers "as a Christian," it is an honor, for it is for the name of Christ (1 Peter 4:16). The word is therefore initially an external term, then it becomes a title of dignity for the believers themselves.
G5546.portee: Being a Christian is not an empty or social label, but a living reality: it is belonging to Christ and bearing His name. This word invites the reader to ask whether their faith in Jesus is authentic and manifest, and to consider the cost — but also the glory — of bearing the name of Christ in a world that is often hostile to Him.

sens: The Anointed One, the one whom God has anointed with holy oil
The Messiah awaited by the Jews, promised Savior and King
Jesus of Nazareth, recognized as the Messiah
The Lord of the Church, Head of the believers
The one in whom resides the salvation and grace of God
G5547.detail: 1. The word comes from the verb "to anoint": it is the one who has been anointed with oil as a sign of divine consecration. In the Old Testament, kings and priests received this anointing to signify that God had chosen them and clothed them with His Spirit (compare 1 Kings 2:10, where it speaks of "the Lord's anointed"). 2. It is the title of the Messiah, the Savior and King that all Israel awaited according to the prophets. The word translates the Hebrew "Messiah": it is the one in whom God's promises for the salvation of His people are fulfilled (Luke 2:11: "for unto you is born this day a Savior, who is Christ"). 3. For the early Christians, this title refers to Jesus of Nazareth Himself: it is the central affirmation of faith (Mark 8:29: "You are the Christ"). His name even becomes inseparable from the title: "Jesus Christ" means "Jesus the Messiah." 4. When Paul speaks of "Christ," he speaks of the one who has conquered sin and death, and who lives in every believer. "For me to live is Christ," he says in Philippians 1:21, showing that Christ is not just a historical figure of the past, but the living Lord of the present. 5. To confess Jesus as Christ is to recognize that in Him dwells complete salvation: grace, forgiveness, new life. He is the center of every divine promise (2 Timothy 1:9: grace was given to us "in Christ Jesus before the ages began").
G5547.origine: The Greek word "Christos" literally means "anointed" (from the verb "chrio" = to anoint). The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it to render the Hebrew word "Messiah" ("Mashiach"), which has exactly the same meaning. The practice of anointing kings and priests with holy oil marked divine choice and the transmission of the Holy Spirit. Gradually, this title became the name of the awaited Deliverer, the one whom God would anoint to save His people. The Jews of Jesus' time spoke of the "Messiah" using this term, and the early believers recognized in Jesus the fulfillment of this promise.
G5547.emploi: The word is ubiquitous in the New Testament (about 529 occurrences). In the Gospels, "Christ" appears either alone or combined with the name "Jesus." The disciples and the crowds question: who is the Christ? Is it Jesus? (Mark 8:29; Luke 2:26). Opponents deny or mock Him (Matthew 27:22; Mark 15:32). In Acts, proclaiming Jesus as Christ is at the heart of apostolic preaching (Acts 2:36: "God has made Him both Lord and Christ"). In Paul, "Christ" or "Jesus Christ" becomes the name of the one in whom God's purpose is fulfilled: justification, sanctification, resurrection. The title retains its dual meaning everywhere: Jesus is the promised Messiah, and also the living Lord in whom believers find their identity and salvation.
G5547.portee: To recognize Jesus as Christ is to believe that God's promises are not in vain, that they are fulfilled in a living and contemporary person. It is to affirm that salvation comes neither from oneself nor from an institution, but from a relationship with the One who bore the weight of sin and death. For every Christian, saying "Christ is my life" (Philippians 1:21) is not a pious formula but an act of radical trust: it is to place one's entire existence under the Lordship of Jesus, to renounce self-salvation, and to accept a new identity in Him.

sens: To pour holy oil on someone as a sign of divine consecration
To entrust someone with a sacred mission, particularly of a king or prophet
To fill someone with the Holy Spirit and His power
G5548.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to pour holy oil on someone's head or body. This was the gesture of the Hebrews to consecrate priests, prophets, and kings to their divine function (Exodus 28:41 for priests, 1 Kings 10:1 for kings). This material gesture marked that the person came under God's hand and received His blessing.
2. Beyond the gesture, to anoint means to entrust someone with a sacred mission and to establish them in a divine office. Jesus says in Luke 4:18: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor." Here, the anointing signifies that God has designated and sent Him to fulfill His mission as Savior.
3. In the New Testament, to anoint becomes primarily the image of the action of the Holy Spirit who fills and strengthens. In Acts 10:38, God "anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power." In 2 Corinthians 1:21, God "has anointed us," meaning He has filled us with His presence and help in Christ.
G5548.origine: The Greek verb chriō comes from the root meaning "to rub" or "to smear." In ancient Greek, it designates the action of pouring oil. The name "Christ" (Christos) derives from it: it literally means "the Anointed One," that is, the one whom God has anointed. In the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew mashakh, which has the same concrete and sacred meaning. That is why all kings, priests, and prophets consecrated by anointing bore the title of "messiah" or "anointed of the Lord."
G5548.emploi: The verb to anoint appears 5 times in the New Testament, always referring to divine action. In Luke 4:18 and Hebrews 1:9, it is applied to Jesus the Messiah, already consecrated by God for His mission. In Acts 4:27 and 10:38, it also qualifies Jesus, showing that the divine anointing is not just a gesture of the past, but reveals the present mission of Christ filled with the Holy Spirit. In 2 Corinthians 1:21, Paul applies it to Christians: God has anointed us, consecrating us in Christ and giving us access to His presence. The meaning thus evolves from the symbolic material gesture to the spiritual reality of the presence and power of the Spirit.
G5548.portee: This word reminds us that our faith in Jesus is faith in God's Anointed One, the one whom God has designated and filled with His Spirit for our salvation. For the Christian, the anointing speaks of consecration to God: we are anointed in Christ, that is, established by God in a new identity and a new power. This assures us that our life belongs to God and that His Spirit strengthens us in our walk of faith.

sens: To take time, to let time pass
To wait a long time, to linger somewhere without rushing
To be late, not to come or arrive at the expected time
To postpone, to defer the accomplishment of something
G5549.detail:
1. The basic meaning is the action of consuming time, letting time flow: it is to spend time, to stay for a moment. In Luke 1:21, Zechariah "was staying" a long time in the temple — he was consuming time, lingering there.

2. From this comes the meaning of waiting slowly, lingering somewhere without haste. This describes the attitude of someone who takes their time, who is not in a hurry to move or act.

3. The main nuance, that of delay, appears when one is waiting for someone or something: to delay is not to come at the expected time. In Matthew 24:48 and Hebrews 10:37, the master or the one who is to come "delays" — he does not arrive when expected. It is the idea of a delay, of non-arrival.

4. To delay can also mean to defer an action, to push it back, to postpone: to refuse to act immediately.
G5549.origine: The word comes from the Greek χρόνος (chronos), which means time — not the decisive moment, but the duration, the passing of hours and days. To delay, therefore, is to "spend time," "consume time." The verbal form adds the idea of action, of an active process. It is a simple but expressive verb: it paints someone who lets time flow without acting, without rushing.
G5549.emploi: The verb appears 5 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew and Luke, with a clear concentration on the idea of delay. In Matthew 24:48 and 25:5, Jesus warns against the servants who think their master "delays" in returning: they take advantage of this supposed delay to do wrong. In Hebrews 10:37, the divine promise states that the one who is to come "will not delay" — an affirmation of His certain and imminent coming. In Luke 1:21 and 12:45, the verb rather describes the act of staying, lingering longer than expected. The word thus always carries a temporal nuance: something or someone does not move at the expected pace.
G5549.portee: This word challenges the Christian reader regarding impatience and trust. When the servant thinks the master "delays," he falls into the trap of disobedience. For the Christian who awaits the return of Christ, to delay becomes a test of faith: to believe that Jesus will come, even if it seems long, and to remain faithful despite the appearance of delay. The verb also warns us against the trap of taking advantage of time to forget our responsibilities.

sens: A duration, long or short, measurable in hours, days, or years
The moment, the instant when something occurs
The historical period or epoch
The occasions and opportunities that God sets
The entire life of a person, their lifespan
Eternity, ages without end
G5550.detail:
1. Chronos primarily designates a span of time: a measurable quantity, whether short or long. Herod wants to know "how long the star has been shining" (Matthew 2:7), that is, how many days or months.
2. It is also the moment when an event occurs: "When they brought a child to Jesus" (Luke 1:57 — at the moment when Elizabeth gave birth), it is the time set by God.
3. Chronos can designate an era or age in history: "in the last days" (1 Peter 1:20), that is, in the time we live, before the return of Christ.
4. In Acts 1:7, "the times or seasons that the Father has fixed" speaks of the times and seasons that God alone determines — the idea that God governs all history.
5. "As long as he lived" (Romans 7:1) shows that it refers to the lifespan of a person, the time they remain alive on earth.
6. Finally, "before the ages began" (2 Timothy 1:9) evokes eternity, the ages without end that precede and follow our existence.
G5550.origine: Chronos comes from an Indo-European root that evokes unfolding, continuity. The Hebrew word "yom" (day) and "ʿet" (moment, occasion) are often translated by chronos in the Greek Old Testament. It is a concrete word: it primarily depicts time that flows, which can be counted and measured.
G5550.emploi: Chronos appears 53 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts, the epistles, and Revelation. It primarily designates a duration or span of time: "For a long time he refused" (Luke 18:4), "they stayed quite a long time with the disciples" (Acts 14:28). It can also name a moment fixed by God: "the times or moments that the Father has fixed" (Acts 1:7). Sometimes it expresses the duration of a person's life: "as long as he lived" (Romans 7:1). The New Testament also plays on the opposition between chronos (the passing time, earthly history) and kairos (the decisive moment, the opportunity given by God), notably in Acts 1:7 and 1 Thessalonians 5:1.
G5550.portee: Chronos reminds the believer that time is a concrete reality, either a resource given by God or a master that governs us. When Scripture speaks of the time that the Father "has fixed" (Acts 1:7), it affirms that history does not escape God, even if we are unaware of it. Understanding this distinction between flowing time and the "times" that God alone determines invites the Christian to wait for the return of Christ with patience, without setting dates.

sens: Spending time staying somewhere or waiting without benefit for one's purpose
Delaying, postponing one's journey by stopping
G5551.detail:
1. This word expresses the idea of wasting or losing time by remaining passive or lingering in one place. The underlying image is that of time passing, consumed without profit. Paul refuses to stop in Ephesus to avoid wasting time in Asia (Acts 20:16), because he must reach Jerusalem before Pentecost: every day counts, every pause becomes a loss.
2. The word also emphasizes the delay caused by a stop: staying somewhere means deferring one's progress toward a goal. In other words, stopping there would waste the necessary time for the journey.
G5551.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: χρόνος (chronos), which refers to the passing of time, and τρίβω (tribō), which means to wear out, rub, consume. The initial image is that of time consumed, worn out, wasted. It is an uncommon compound word in Greek, formed to precisely describe this idea: seeing time pass without profit. No Hebrew word corresponds exactly to this usage, as it is a typically Mediterranean Greek construction.
G5551.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:16. Paul, returning from his third missionary journey, must choose between stopping in Ephesus (where the Christians of the church he founded live) and quickly continuing to Jerusalem. He rejects the first option precisely to avoid wasting time. This context shows that the word describes not only the sterile passage of time but also a strategic decision: sometimes, stopping, even for good, delays the accomplishment of a priority mission.
G5551.portee: This passage invites the Christian to reflect on the use of time: there is a right balance between investing locally and advancing toward spiritual priorities. Paul does not consider Ephesus as worthless, but he recognizes that the moment requires haste toward an important appointment. This speaks to the modern believer who must discern their priorities and accept that not doing everything is not a loss, but wisdom.

sens: Covered with gold, made of gold or in gold
Shining like gold, resplendent
Figuratively: precious, of great value
G5552.detail:
1. The word primarily describes an object materially composed of gold or covered with a layer of gold. In the heavenly temple described by John, the lampstands, altars, bowls, and trumpets are golden (Revelation 1:12-13, Revelation 8:3): this indicates that these objects belong to the divine realm and are intended for worship. The mention of golden objects and earthenware objects in the same house in 2 Timothy 2:20 shows that "golden" also denotes what is of value and dignity.
2. Gold naturally evokes brilliance and splendor: golden objects shine. When Revelation speaks of the golden crown of Christ (Revelation 14:14) or the golden crowns of the elders around the throne (Revelation 4:4), it signifies their glory and radiant royalty.
3. Sometimes the word carries a deeper symbolic charge: what is golden is precious, permanent, worthy of heaven. The walls and gates of the heavenly Jerusalem made of pure gold (Revelation 21:15) express that this city is the supreme good, incorruptible and eternal.
G5552.origine: The Greek word χρύσεος comes from χρυσός (gold, the metal), which primarily denotes the raw material. In Hebrew, זָהָב (zahab) carries the same meaning: gold as a precious metal, a symbol of wealth and purity. The Greek adjective χρύσεος, regularly formed from this root, means "that is in gold, that contains gold." Gold in the ancient Bible was the most precious good, reserved for the temple and royalty, which explains why this word quickly acquires a theological significance.
G5552.emploi: The word "golden" appears 16 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Revelation of John. It focuses on the symbolic visions of heaven and the heavenly temple: the golden lampstands (1:12), the golden altar (8:3), the golden bowls (5:8), the golden trumpets (9:13). Only one occurrence stands out from this visionary context: 2 Timothy 2:20, where golden vessels and earthenware vessels in a large house illustrate that some are for honor and others for dishonor. In Hebrews 9:4, the golden altar of the Old Testament is mentioned as part of the earthly tabernacle. The usage thus concentrates in the language of apocalyptic vision, where gold symbolizes divine majesty and eternity.
G5552.portee: For the Christian reader, "golden" in Revelation signals that we are reading descriptions of God's world: what shines with gold belongs to the heavenly reality, to God's heaven. This teaches us that divine splendor is real and accessible by faith. When the vision mentions heaven in gold, it invites us to contemplate and desire this eternal beauty that will one day be manifest. Golden gold reminds us that everything that comes from God is worthy of honor and will never pass away.

sens: Precious yellow metal, used to make valuable objects
Object or ornament made of gold
Gold currency, wealth
Construction or base material in a work
G5553.detail:
1. The word denotes gold as raw or worked metal: the precious yellow metal itself, as found or used. In Hebrews 9:4, gold adorns the ark of the covenant; in Revelation 21:18, the wall of the heavenly city is made of pure gold, symbolizing its beauty and perfection.
2. By extension, it refers to the adornments and ornaments in gold worn by wealthy people: necklaces, bracelets, rings. In 1 Timothy 2:9 and 1 Peter 3:3, Paul and Peter advise women against gold jewelry as a sign of ostentation, preferring inner adornment.
3. The word can also refer to gold as currency, a symbol of material wealth and possession. In Acts 3:6, Peter tells the beggar: "Silver and gold, I do not have"; in 1 Peter 1:18, Paul reminds that Christians were redeemed "not with perishable things, like silver or gold".
4. Metaphorically, in 1 Corinthians 3:12, gold figures among the foundation materials of a work — more precious and durable than wood or straw — to represent a solid faith and service that withstands the test of divine judgment.
G5553.origine: The Greek word χρυσίον is a diminutive of χρυσός ("gold"), which literally expresses the idea of a piece or parcel of gold. The Hebrew word זָהָב (zahab), which the Greek gold regularly translates in the Old Testament, carries the same concrete meaning. The root refers to the warmth and brilliance of the metal — gold shines and attracts the eye — which explains its symbolic use for anything precious, durable, and beautiful.
G5553.emploi: This word appears about 12 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles and Revelation. Gold there takes on several roles: object of worship and liturgy (golden altar, ark of the covenant), sign of material wealth that Christians should not idolize, adornment material that believing women can wear discreetly, and symbol of the indestructible and precious nature of faith and Christian work. In Revelation, gold is associated with heavenly glory and perfection — the streets of the New Jerusalem are of pure gold — revealing the priceless value of the Kingdom of God.
G5553.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that material wealth, while not inherently bad, should not become the object of our worship or trust. Gold also symbolizes the purity and preciousness of authentic faith, which alone endures eternally. Finally, the contrast between the corruptible gold of this world and the incorruptible gold of the heavenly city invites us to relativize temporal goods and set our hearts on what is true, just, and eternal.

sens: who wears a gold ring
man of apparent wealth and dignity
G5554.detail:
1. The word literally designates a person adorned with a gold ring. In James 2:2, the apostle imagines a man entering the assembly of Christians "with a gold ring and fine clothes," visible symbols of his wealth and social status.
2. Figuratively, it is the very image of prosperity and prestige: one who wears gold on his fingers displays his fortune and rank. James makes it the emblem of the rich who may receive more honor in the Church than he spiritually deserves.
G5554.origine: The word combines χρυσός (gold, precious metal) and δάκτυλος (finger). It is a compound adjective, forged to describe one who stands out by his gold adornments. This image of the gold ring recalls the Old Testament, where a ring is often a sign of power and authority (as in Genesis 41:42, where Pharaoh gives his ring to Joseph). Here, it becomes the symbol of worldly prestige and wealth.
G5554.emploi: The word appears only once in the entire New Testament, in James 2:2. The apostle uses it to contrast two visitors to the Christian assembly: the man with gold rings, rich and well-dressed, and the poor man in rags. This unique occurrence raises the crucial question: how does the Church treat people based on their outward appearance? James denounces this injustice.
G5554.portee: This word invites the believer to examine his prejudices. In the context of James 2, it reminds us that true value is not measured by the gold one wears, but by the heart. Recognizing appearances as deceptive and decisive in judging others is a call to justice and impartiality in the life of the Church.

sens: precious stone of yellow-green or golden yellow color
G5555.detail: 1. The chrysolite is a translucent precious stone, yellow-green or golden yellow in hue. It is probably peridot or olivine, a gem valued in antiquity. It appears in the list of the twelve precious stones that adorn the foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20), where it is the seventh stone named.
G5555.origine: The Greek word "chrysolithe" comes from two roots: "chrysos" (gold) and "lithos" (stone), literally "golden stone." This compound describes the golden or yellow-green appearance of the gem. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew word "tarschich" (תַּרְשִׁישׁ), which designates a precious stone used in the high priest's garment and in the description of divine glory in Ezekiel.
G5555.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:20. John lists the twelve precious stones that form the foundations of the New Jerusalem. Each stone symbolizes the beauty and eternal splendor of God's city. The chrysolite occupies the seventh place in this prestigious list, attesting to its prestige in the ancient world.
G5555.portee: This enumeration of precious stones in the description of the heavenly Jerusalem reminds the believer that God's eternal kingdom will be of incomparable beauty, surpassing all that we know on earth. These gems symbolize the purity, solidity, and everlasting glory of the eternal dwelling with God.

sens: green to golden yellow precious stone
stone used to adorn the heavenly Jerusalem
G5556.detail:
1. Chrysoprase is a precious stone that is green with yellow or golden reflections. Its Greek name literally means "gold-leek" ("chryso" = gold, "prasos" = leek), as it resembles the hue of a golden leek. It is a variety of chalcedony, a fairly common stone but valued for its luster and beauty.
2. In Revelation, John lists twelve precious stones that adorn the twelve foundations of the heavenly Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20). Chrysoprase is the tenth stone in this list, symbolizing the beauty, wealth, and holiness of God's City. These stones represent the perfection and glory of the divine edifice.
G5556.origine: The Greek word "chrysoprasos" is composed of two elements: "chryso-" (gold) and "prasos" (leek). This combination describes the appearance of the stone, whose green hue leans towards gold, hence its resemblance to the color of an aureoled leek. The Greeks coined this name by observing the natural appearance of the stone, thus translating the clarity of its visual description.
G5556.emploi: The word "chrysoprasos" appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 21:20, where John describes the foundations of the new Jerusalem. It appears in a list of twelve precious stones that constitute the twelve foundations of the holy city's wall. This unique presence in Revelation shows that John draws from the vocabulary of gems and minerals known in his time to depict the splendor of the world to come.
G5556.portee: For the believer, this precious stone reminds us that the eternal dwelling promised by God will be of incomparable beauty and perfectly adorned. Each stone listed in the heavenly Jerusalem invites contemplation of the wealth and magnificence of the blessed reality that awaits those who persevere in faith.

sens: the precious yellow, shiny, and unchanging metal
a gold coin
an object made of gold: ornament, jewel, image, or vase
wealth, the accumulation of material goods
what is precious and perishable before God
G5557.detail:
1. The metal gold itself, coveted since antiquity for its beauty and rarity: the Magi bring gold among their gifts to the Christ child (Matthew 2:11), a symbol of his royalty.
2. A gold coin, a common form of circulating wealth: Jesus forbids his apostles from taking gold in their purse when he sends them to proclaim the Gospel (Matthew 10:9), thus inviting them to trust in God.
3. Any object manufactured from gold: the ornaments worn by women (1 Timothy 2:9), the cups and objects of the temple that the Pharisees wonder whether to swear by (Matthew 23:16-17), the idols (Acts 17:29), or the precious vessels of great Babylon (Revelation 18:12) — gold becomes the symbol of luxury and human prestige.
4. By extension, the accumulated material wealth, an object of worldly desire and concern: James denounces the gold that rusts as a testimony against those who have acquired it unjustly (James 5:3).
5. Metaphorically, what is precious but earthly and destructible, in contrast to what lasts eternally: in the vision of Babylon, the gold of the walls announced as destroyed (Revelation 18:12) reminds us that the splendor of the world passes away.
G5557.origine: The Greek word χρυσός comes from an Indo-European root meaning what shines or glitters. It translates the Hebrew זָהָב (zahav), attested since antiquity to designate this precious metal known to the Hebrews since Abraham. Gold was never invented by the Greeks: it is a natural good, an element of the created world that man discovers and uses. The word remains identical in classical Greek, koine, and modern Greek.
G5557.emploi: The word appears about 9 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Gospel of Matthew (Magi, coin, temple), Acts (idolatry), the epistles of Paul and James (wealth, luxury), and Revelation (symbol of earthly prosperity). Matthew uses it for the true treasure (the gold of the Magi) and false treasures (the temple, the coin); James and Revelation imbue it with irony: the gold that rusts and the gold that collapses remind us that material wealth does not save. Paul speaks of it simply as a building material (1 Corinthians 3:12), where each one builds on the foundation that is Christ. No moral judgment on the metal itself, but on what man makes of it: an object of idolatry or proof of his vanity.
G5557.portee: Gold in the Bible is never bad in itself — it is a treasure from God — but it becomes a trap when coveted or preferred over the word of God. For the Christian reader, this word invites discernment: where do you place your heart? Do you seek the earthly gold that rusts and can be stolen, or the incorruptible inheritance? The Magi bring gold to Jesus because they recognized his true value; the disciple must do the same, not by abandoning possessions (which may come from God), but by refusing to let wealth become his master or god.

sens: To cover or adorn with gold
To dress in wealth and splendor
G5558.detail:
1. The word literally means to cover something with a layer of gold, as one would do with a varnish or gilding: it is applying gold to a surface to beautify it. In Revelation 17:4, the woman is "adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls" — the gold here is not the substance itself, but the ornament added, the adornment.
2. Figuratively, the word extends to the broader idea of dressing someone or something in wealth and splendor. The great city in Revelation 18:16 is adorned "with gold, precious stones, and pearls," images of its brazen prosperity and pride: the gilding becomes a symbol of superficial beauty based on material wealth.
G5558.origine: The verb comes from χρυσός (gold, the precious metal). It is a verb of transformation: it expresses the action of dressing something with what makes it precious in the eyes of the world. The family of words related to gold runs throughout Scripture as a symbol of what shines, seduces, and tempts.
G5558.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in Revelation (17:4 and 18:16). In these two passages, John describes a woman dressed in sumptuous silks and adorned with solid gold. The word emphasizes the contrast between apparent brilliance and hidden corruption: this golden adornment is merely a superficial layer that covers the "abominations" and "impurity" (Revelation 17:4). The repeated use suggests that gilding is a trap, the bait of a seduction that dazzles the eyes.
G5558.portee: This verb invites the reader to pierce through appearances: what shines with gold is not necessarily pure or true. The golden adornment of apocalyptic Babylon warns us against the illusion that material wealth would be a sign of purity or divine favor. It is a lesson in spiritual discernment: to look beyond the splendor to see the hidden moral reality beneath.

sens: the surface of the human body, covered with flesh
figuratively: the whole person, the living body
G5559.detail:
1. The skin is the outer surface of the body, which covers it. In Acts 19:12, the text speaks of cloths that had touched the skin (the body) of Paul: it is this cutaneous surface, this physical envelope that is in contact with clothing and through which divine virtue can be transmitted.
2. By extension, the word designates the whole body as it is living and visible. When the cloths had touched Paul, it was his physical person, his entire body in its fleshly presence, that was at stake — not an abstraction, but what is tangible and observable.
G5559.origine: The Greek word chrôs literally means skin, the visible surface of the body. It comes from an ancient root and mainly appears in classical poetry; biblical prose rarely employs it. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it generally renders the Hebrew word "flesh" (basar), which encompasses the physical body in its entirety.
G5559.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 19:12, at the heart of the account of the miracles performed by Paul in Ephesus. In this context, "touching his skin" literally means that the cloths and handkerchiefs had been in contact with the apostle's body. It is this physical contact with Paul's body that becomes the vector of a healing virtue — diseases leave the sick and evil spirits come out of those who carried these cloths. The use thus emphasizes the reality of the living body as a means of transmitting divine power.
G5559.portee: This word reminds us that God does not disdain the physical body: He acts through it, touches it, heals it. It is an invitation to recognize that biblical faith is not purely spiritual or abstract — it passes through the concrete, through hands, through fleshly presence, through contact. The body is not an obstacle to divine power, but an instrument and an object of His mercy.

sens: who cannot walk normally because a leg or foot is impaired or paralyzed
a person excluded from certain places or services because of this impairment
miraculously healed of this impairment
G5560.detail:
1. The word literally describes someone whose leg or foot does not function properly, who limps or can only walk with difficulty. In Acts 3:2, it is the man "lame from birth, whom they carried and placed every day at the gate of the temple": he depended entirely on others for movement.
2. In the Old Testament, such an impairment rendered access to temple service impossible (Leviticus 21:18 in the Hebrew Bible). That is why this man remained outside at the Beautiful Gate, excluded from worship.
3. The Bible associates the healing of the lame with the miracles of Jesus and the apostles: this shows that the Kingdom of God heals and restores. In Matthew 11:5 and Luke 7:22, Jesus lists the restored walking of the lame among the signs that the Messiah has brought. In Acts 3:2-11 and 14:8, the apostles also heal the lame, continuing the work of Jesus.
G5560.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to limp" or "to be lame"; it describes the state of the body, not a moral judgment. In Acts 3:2, it appears alongside terms for blindness and other impairments. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it often renders the Hebrew word פִּסֵּחַ (pisséah), "lame," from the verb meaning "to limp."
G5560.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, almost always in the Gospels and Acts. It appears in three main contexts: (1) the lists of miracles of Jesus (Matthew 11:5, 15:30-31; Luke 7:22; Matthew 21:14), where the lame walk just as the blind see; (2) the detailed account of the healing of the lame man at the Beautiful Gate in Acts 3:2, where Peter and John restore him to full mobility; (3) the images of the Kingdom in the parables (Luke 14:13, 14:21), where the lame are expressly invited to the feast. Hebrews 12:13 uses the word figuratively: "make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be dislocated, but rather be healed," meaning to strengthen the weak.
G5560.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus, in His ministry and after His resurrection through the apostles, heals infirmities: He does not ignore the marginalized and the excluded. For today's believer, it is a sign that the Kingdom of God restores physical integrity and human dignity. It is also an invitation to welcome and serve those whom society looks down upon.

sens: region, land, territory
inhabited land, domain
cultivated field, agricultural land
the collective inhabitants of a region
G5561.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a region or geographical territory, often with its inhabitants: it is a defined space with its own characteristics. For example, Mark 5:1 speaks of the "country of the Gerasenes," a specific area near the sea.
2. It is also used for land, a property owned: Luke 12:16 tells the story of a rich man whose "land" (his property) produced abundantly.
3. The word can refer to cultivated fields, agricultural land, in contrast to the city: John 4:35 invites Jesus to "lift up your eyes and look at the fields that are white for harvest."
4. Finally, "country" can refer to its inhabitants, to the community that occupies it: Acts 10:39 speaks of all that Jesus "did in the country of the Jews."
G5561.origine: The Greek word chōra comes from a root meaning space, place: it is primarily a concept of territorial extension. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it to translate the Hebrew eretz ("land") and médinah ("region, province"). Chōra belongs to a family of Greek words related to the notion of space: chōros ("place"), chōreúō ("to advance, to move").
G5561.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and Acts. It often describes regions of Palestine: Judea, Galilee, the Trachonitis, the country of the Gerasenes. But it is also used for any territory (Matthew 2:12, the country of the Magi). Luke frequently uses this word to contrast the countryside and the city (Luke 21:21: "those who are in the fields"). In Luke 15:14-15 (the prodigal son), "country" takes on a moral connotation: it is the distant land where the young man goes astray. The word can also refer to a rural property or its agricultural income.
G5561.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus incarnated in a concrete geographical setting: he walked in countries, visited regions, met specific peoples. For the Christian, this shows that the Gospel is not an abstract message, but rooted in history and land. The notion of "country" also invites reflection on our belonging: not only to a physical land, but to an eternal Kingdom that does not pass away.

sens: Make room, leave space
Receive, welcome in a physical space
Hold, be able to retain a certain quantity
Accept, receive mentally or spiritually
Welcome, find a place in the heart or mind
G5562.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make room, to yield ground, to step aside: the idea is that something or someone withdraws to allow others to advance or settle.
2. The verb then means to receive, to physically welcome: a house, a room, a container that receives people or things. Mark 2:2 illustrates this reality well: the crowd is so numerous that the space in front of the door can no longer contain them.
3. Concretely, it is to have the capacity to hold, to retain a determined quantity: John 2:6 speaks of the jars used for purification that each contained two or three measures.
4. In a figurative and spiritual sense, it is to receive a word, an idea, a truth in one's understanding or heart. Matthew 19:11: "Not everyone understands this saying," where to understand means to let the word enter oneself to grasp it.
5. More broadly, it is to welcome, accept something immaterial into one's being: John 8:37 says that the word of Jesus does not penetrate (does not find a place) in those who refuse to hear it.
G5562.origine: The Greek verb χωρέω comes from a root meaning "space," "place." The Greek word χῶρος (chôros) designates space, place, region. The verb thus originally expresses the idea of moving in space, making room, holding place. This spatial image naturally extends to the intellectual and spiritual domain: making room for a thought means receiving it in one's heart and mind.
G5562.emploi: The verb χωρέω appears about nine times in the New Testament, especially in John and Matthew. In the Gospels, it is used both in the concrete sense (to contain people or things: Mark 2:2, John 2:6, John 21:25) and in the spiritual and intellectual sense (to understand, to welcome a word or truth: Matthew 19:11-12, John 8:37). In 2 Corinthians 7:2, Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him in their hearts. In 2 Peter 3:9, God "is patient" with sinners, which is expressed by the fact that he "gives time" for them to repent. The meaning varies according to the context but always revolves around the idea of receiving, welcoming, giving place.
G5562.portee: This word teaches us that receiving the word of God is first about making room for it within us, consenting to give it space in our hearts and minds. It shows us that faith is not passive: it requires an openness, an inner availability. It also reminds us that not all hearts are equally disposed to welcome divine truth, and that it is a grace to be able to "understand" and "contain" the mysteries of God.

sens: divide into two, place on one side and the other
remove someone from something or someone
leave a place, go away
break a marriage or union
be distinct, without connection
G5563.detail:
1. To separate in the most concrete sense: to place on one side and the other what was together. This is what should not be done in marriage: "Therefore what God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matthew 19:6). The image is that of sharing, of division into two.
2. To remove someone from a place or a person. Jesus advises the disciples "not to depart from Jerusalem" (Acts 1:4), meaning not to leave that city. It is the action of putting at a distance.
3. To leave, to depart from a place. When Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, he "departed from Athens" (Acts 18:1). The word describes the movement of departure, without emphasis on rupture.
4. To break a marriage or union. Paul addresses divorce in 1 Corinthians 7 by speaking of spouses who "separate": it is the breaking of a marital bond.
5. To be unable to separate, to detach. Nothing can "separate us from the love of God" (Romans 8:39): the verb in the negative form expresses the absolute impossibility of breaking this divine bond.
G5563.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that evokes the idea of making an interval, creating space. It is found in French in "choreography" (arrangement of the space of dance). In Hebrew, the corresponding verb in the Septuagint is often bâdal, which means "to set apart, to distinguish." The family of the word also includes "chorîzô" (separation) and compound words with the prefix "apo-" (to separate from).
G5563.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament. In Matthew and Mark, it designates the prohibition of separating spouses (19:6 and 10:9), where the verb in the present tense affirms an immutable principle. In Romans 8, Paul forcefully asks, "Who will separate us?" from the love of Christ: the repetition in 8:35 and 8:39 shows that this separation is impossible, it is the touchstone of the believer's certainty. In Acts, the verb simply means "to leave" or "to distance oneself" (1:4, 18:1-2). In 1 Corinthians 7, it describes divorce or marital separation, in a pastoral context where Paul regulates this practice. The word consistently retains this fundamental meaning: to create distance, to break proximity or a bond.
G5563.portee: This word reminds us that sacred bonds — especially marriage — should not be broken lightly, since God has united them. More profoundly, the repetition of "separate" in Romans 8:35-39 becomes an announcement of joy: no circumstance, no force in the world can tear us away from the love of God. It is a word of comfort for the tested Christian, who can remain calm: he will never be separated from his Lord.

sens: A place, a location, a region
A property, an estate, a cultivated or inhabited plot of land
G5564G.detail:
1. The word primarily designates simply a place or a specific location on earth: thus Jesus goes to pray in a "place" called Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36, Mark 14:32), a garden outside Jerusalem. This is the most neutral and broad meaning of the word.
2. More concretely, it refers to real estate, a plot of land that one owns: it can be a cultivated field, like the one Jacob gave to Joseph (John 4:5), or an urban lot, like the field of Hakeldama purchased with the price of Judas's crime (Acts 1:18-19). The disciples sold their fields and houses to share the proceeds with the poor (Acts 4:34), which shows that it was a concrete and valuable wealth.
G5564G.origine: The Greek word χωρίον is a diminutive of χώρα or χῶρος, which mean "space," "place," or "country." The diminutive suggests a limited portion of space — a plot rather than a vast territory. It is a common word in Greek to designate a property, an estate, or a small well-defined territory, whether cultivated or inhabited.
G5564G.emploi: The word appears nine times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and in Acts. In the Gospels, it designates a specific geographical location: the garden of Gethsemane where Jesus prays before his arrest. In Acts, it often takes on the more concrete meaning of real estate or field: the field of Hakeldama purchased by Judas (Acts 1:18-19), the fields that believers sold as a sign of brotherly sharing (Acts 4:34, 5:3, 5:8), or the field that belonged to Publius, the main character in Malta (Acts 28:7). The meaning remains constant: a defined portion of land, owned and generally productive.
G5564G.portee: This word reminds us that in the life of the early Church, land and material goods are concrete realities that can serve the love of one's neighbor. The disciples do not jealously keep their fields and houses, but sell them to help the poor — it is an act of generosity and communion. The word also invites the reader to see Jesus in a real place, a real garden where he suffered, thus anchoring his prayer and sacrifice in actual history.

sens: a small plot of land, a real estate property
a defined area or region
figuratively, a domain or field of action
G5564H.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a small plot or land that one owns: it is a property, often agricultural. In Acts 1:19, it refers to the "field of blood" — the land that the apostles bought with the money given by Judas, and where he was to be buried according to God's plan.
2. More broadly, it is a territory or a specific place, a defined region in which something happens or exists. It conveys the idea of concrete and bounded space.
3. By extension, the word can evoke a field of activity or a space where one acts — the field that God opens, or the one where one labors.
G5564H.origine: The Greek word comes from a root denoting space, region, and it is formed as a diminutive (an affectionate or reducing form) of « χώρα » (chôra), which means "country" or "territory." This root evokes the idea of a measurable and defined space — which makes the field seen as a part of the soil that can be circumscribed and exploited. In the Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew « כֶּרֶם » (kerèm), which means vineyard or orchard — that is, a cultivated land bearing fruit.
G5564H.emploi: The word appears mainly in the New Testament to designate land properties or specific places. In Acts 1:19, the context is that of Judas's remorse and death: the field of blood becomes a terrible memorial, known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem. It is a real place, geographically identified, that carries within it the history of betrayal and divine judgment. The term emphasizes the materiality of the fact: it truly exists, people designate it, it has a name in the language of the people.
G5564H.portee: This passage reminds us that God controls history even in its darkest details. The "field of blood" is not an abstraction: it is a visible place, a silent testimony to the price of sin and sovereign grace. For the believer, it is an invitation to see that God transforms even places marked by betrayal into signs of His justice and forgiveness.

sens: apart from, separated from
devoid of, lacking
in the absence of, without the help of
except, excluding
G5565.detail:
1. The primary meaning is spatial or concrete: to be apart from something, separated from it. John 20:7 provides an example: the linen that wrapped Jesus is folded "apart," separated from the other linens.
2. The most common meaning is that of deprivation or absence: lacking something, being devoid of it. Ephesians 2:12 expresses this strongly: the Gentiles were "without Christ," lacking His presence and promises.
3. The word also denotes the absence of a necessary condition or means: not having what is essential to act or exist. John 15:5 illustrates this perfectly: "without me you can do nothing" — without the life that Jesus gives, the disciples are powerless.
4. Sometimes the word means "except" or "excluding": it excludes something from the following proposition. Hebrews 7:7 states that it is "without dispute" that the inferior receives the blessing from the superior — it is an exclusion of doubt.
G5565.origine: The Greek word χωρίς comes from a root expressing the idea of space or separation. It belongs to the family of prepositions that mark absence or distinction. As a preposition followed by the genitive (the case of the possessor), it often translates the Hebrew « בִלְתִּי » ("without, except"). It is an equivalent of the word ἄνευ, which has the same meaning.
G5565.emploi: The word χωρίς appears 38 times in the New Testament, notably in Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, and in James. In the Gospels, it marks the absence of means or condition: Jesus spoke "without parable" (Matthew 13:34), meaning He did not speak without using parables. In Paul, particularly in Romans 3-7, the word expresses what it is "without the law" or "without Christ" — the previous state, without divine help. In Hebrews 9-10, it describes elements of the ancient worship: sacrifice "without shedding of blood," offerings "without mercy." The word can also mean "except" or "outside of": in Hebrews 12:14, the vision of God does not occur "without holiness." It is a very useful preposition for the theology of the New Testament.
G5565.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize his absolute dependence on Christ and on God's grace. John 15:5 teaches that in oneself, without the life that Jesus gives, we can bear no lasting fruit. In Ephesians 2:12, remembering having been "without Christ" reveals what the Gospel means: it gives us access to what we lacked. It is a word to meditate on for prayer and for trust in God.

sens: the wind blowing from the northwest
the direction of northwest
G5566.detail:
1. The word designates the wind that comes from the northwest — one of the main directions of the ancient maritime compass. In Acts 27:12, Paul and his companions discuss the ports of Crete: Phoenix "looks toward the southwest and the northwest," meaning that its openings face these two directions of the sea, where these winds blow.
2. By extension, it simply designates the direction of northwest itself, the region or point on the horizon located between north and west.
G5566.origine: The Greek word χῶρος (chôros) comes from a root that designates space, place, or direction. Here, in the maritime context, it takes up the Latin name for the northwest wind, Caurus, adapted to Greek. It is a technical term from ancient nautical vocabulary, rarely found in biblical texts.
G5566.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:12. Paul is aboard a ship en route to Rome; the crew is looking for a good port to winter in Crete. The mention of northwest is precise: it describes the orientation of the port of Phoenix, which faces both southwest and northwest, in order to understand the winds and tides. It is a concrete nautical detail that testifies to the author's knowledge of Mediterranean navigation.
G5566.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks of the real world, with its precise geographical and technical details. It is not limited to religious teachings, but roots the history of salvation in the concrete history of people and their journeys.

sens: to make the strings of a musical instrument sound by plucking them with the fingers
to perform a melody by singing, especially psalms or hymns
to praise God through song
to express joy or gladness by singing
G5567.detail:
1. The word first evokes the physical action of making the strings of an instrument vibrate: one pulls or plucks the strings to produce sound, as one would make the string of a bow vibrate (Romans 15:9 shows Paul singing "to the glory of the name" of the Lord).
2. More broadly, "to sing" means to produce a melody with one's voice, often accompanied by a musical instrument. In 1 Corinthians 14:15, Paul clearly distinguishes singing "with the spirit" (with divine inspiration) and singing "with the understanding" (with comprehension of the meaning).
3. Singing becomes an act of praise to God: it is celebrating His greatness and love. Ephesians 5:19 exhorts believers to speak to one another "with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody with all your heart to the Lord."
4. Singing can also express the inner joy of a believer. James 5:13 invites anyone who is "cheerful" to "sing psalms," as a natural manifestation of happiness in God.
G5567.origine: The Greek word psallō comes from the verb that literally means "to pluck, to make vibrate" (as one plucks a string). In Hebrew, it primarily translates two verbs: zamár (to sing, to make music) and nagán (to play an instrument). These Hebrew roots were already associated with cultic praise and joy in the Psalms. The transition from the simple plucking of strings to singing praise shows how a physical gesture becomes a spiritual act.
G5567.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Pauline epistles and in James. In Romans 15:9, Paul cites a passage from the Old Testament where he commits to singing the praises of God among the Gentiles. In 1 Corinthians 14:15, the context of spiritual gifts shows that singing must be accompanied by understanding (not just emotion). In Ephesians 5:19, the collective singing of believers is presented as a discipline of common spiritual life, a means of edifying one another. In James 5:13, singing appears as the joyful response of the believer to God's goodness. In all cases, it is always about singing in a religious or spiritual context, never about secular music.
G5567.portee: For the believer, "to sing" is not entertainment but an act of communion with God and with the Church. It is the expression of Christian joy and a means of proclaiming God's praise. The New Testament shows that spiritual singing must be thoughtful and inspired by the Spirit, while also springing from the heart (Ephesians 5:19). Thus, music becomes a discipline of faith, capable of transforming personal and communal worship.

sens: A musical composition sung with accompaniment of stringed instruments
A sacred song or hymn intended for praise and edification
Specifically, one of the 150 poems in the Book of Psalms of the Old Testament
G5568.detail:
1. Originally, the word psalm designates the act of striking the strings of an instrument — the very image of sound bursting forth. This is why it refers to a musical composition sung with instrumental accompaniment, never without music. In 1 Corinthians 14:26, during gatherings, a brother may bring "a song" (psalm) to edify the church.
2. In the life of the Church, a psalm is a sacred song that nourishes faith and common edification. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16, Paul exhorts Christians to "speak to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs" to cultivate wisdom and praise the Lord together.
3. The psalm also refers, and especially, to the 150 sung poems of the Book of Psalms. The risen Jesus tells His disciples (Luke 24:44) that everything must be fulfilled "in the law of Moses, in the prophets, and in the psalms" — three divisions of Scripture. David himself is cited as the author of the Psalms (Luke 20:42 and Acts 1:20).
G5568.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "psallô" which means to strike or pluck the strings. This root emphasizes that the psalm is never a silent poetry: it is a word accompanied by instrumental music. In the Greek Old Testament, "psalm" translates the Hebrew "mizmôr" (מִזְמוֹר), which carries the same meaning: a song intended to be played and sung.
G5568.emploi: The word appears seven times in the New Testament. It primarily designates the songs that Christians compose or recite to edify one another in gatherings (1 Corinthians 14:26). It also refers to the hymns and songs of praise that Paul encourages to be sung (Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16). Finally, and mainly, it designates the Book of Psalms of the Old Testament. Jesus says that everything concerning Him is fulfilled "in the psalms" (Luke 24:44), and Peter cites the Book of Psalms as sacred Scripture (Acts 1:20). The psalms are thus prophetic texts announcing Christ.
G5568.portee: For the Christian, the psalm reminds us that the praise of God is never a purely intellectual or silent matter: it engages the heart, the voice, and the instrument. It is a means of communion with God and other believers. The Psalms of the Old Testament remain an inexhaustible source for expressing true emotions before God — joy, distress, trust, repentance — and for discovering how Jesus was foretold in every age of history.

sens: One who pretends to be a Christian but is not truly one
One who has secretly slipped among the disciples with bad intentions
One who threatens the unity and freedom of the Christian assembly
G5569.detail:
1. A false brother is someone who pretends to be a Christian, who speaks the language of faith, but whose heart and actions do not correspond to this profession. Paul mentions these false brothers among the perils he faced during his missionary journeys in 2 Corinthians 11:26: they are as real a danger as robbers or swollen rivers.
2. It is particularly someone who has discreetly "introduced" themselves into the assembly, as Paul explains in Galatians 2:4: these false brothers have "slipped in among" the Christians, hiding their true objectives.
3. Their aim is to harm the freedom of true believers and to "enslave" them — they seek to impose rules or practices that contradict the Gospel of grace, such as the observance of the Jewish Law that some wanted to force upon Christians from paganism.
G5569.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "pseudo" (false, deceptive) and "adelphos" (brother). The root "adelphos" comes from an ancient Indo-European root meaning one who is born from the same womb. "Pseudo" refers to the idea of something that is merely an appearance, a counterfeit. The word thus expresses the idea of a usurped, counterfeit brotherly relationship: someone who claims to belong to the Christian family without having the heart for it.
G5569.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, and always in Paul's writings. In 2 Corinthians 11:26, in a list of perils, Paul cites false brothers as a legitimate threat alongside robbers or storms: it is a concrete and serious danger. In Galatians 2:4, the context is more specific: these false brothers are Judaizers, men who had "secretly infiltrated" to "spy" on Christian freedom and force converts to observe Jewish customs. In both cases, they are people who claim to share the faith but pursue objectives contrary to the Gospel.
G5569.portee: This word invites Christians to spiritual vigilance: faith is not a matter of appearance or words, but of a transformed heart. It also reminds us that the Christian assembly can be infiltrated by people who threaten its freedom and unity. Finally, it exhorts us to discern who our true brothers and sisters in Christ are, not through condemning judgment, but through discerning the fruits and faithfulness to the Gospel.

sens: someone who claims to be an apostle of Christ without truly being one
a religious impostor who deceives by false appearances
