a worker of lies disguised as an authentic messenger of the Gospel
G5570.detail:
1. A false apostle is someone who claims to be an apostle of Christ — a direct envoy of the Lord with authority to teach and lead the Church — while he is not. He is an impostor who usurps a position he has not received.

2. The word evokes a disguise: like a false prophet or a false messiah, the false apostle deceives others by presenting himself under a false identity. In 2 Corinthians 11:13, Paul describes these impostors as "deceitful workers, disguised as apostles of Christ" — they wear the mask of apostleship to better seduce the Christians of Corinth.

3. Above all, he is a worker of lies: not someone ignorant, but someone who actively and knowingly works to deceive the faithful by distorting the message of the Gospel and usurping apostolic authority.
G5570.origine: The word is composed of two elements: the prefix "pseudo-" (ψευδ-) meaning "false" or "lying," and "apostolos" (ἀπόστολος), which means "sent one" or "apostle." The root of the word "apostolos" comes from the verb "apostellein" (ἀποστέλλειν) meaning "to send on a mission." Together, "pseudapostolos" literally designates a "false sent one," an impostor who claims a mission he has never received from Christ.
G5570.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Corinthians 11:13. Paul uses it to denounce the adversaries who troubled the Church of Corinth. These false apostles presented themselves as workers of Christ, but Paul exposes them as deceivers seeking to mislead the faithful. The context shows that Paul opposes those who question his apostolic authority and that of his collaborators. The word emphasizes that these impostors are not merely misinformed men, but active adversaries of the true Gospel who manipulate believers with deceptive words.
G5570.portee: This passage helps Christians recognize false teachers: not by their appearance or enticing promises, but by the conformity of their message with the authentic Gospel and their true submission to Christ. Paul also invites every believer to vigilance: religious deception exists, and it is all the more formidable as it disguises itself as truth. That is why scrutinizing the Scriptures and knowing true doctrine are not merely theoretical exercises, but an essential protection against seduction.

sens: One who lies, who tells falsehoods
One who is contrary to the truth, false
One who deceives or misleads
G5571.detail:
1. A liar is someone who utters intentional lies — he speaks against the truth knowingly. In Revelation 2:2, the Lord praises the church of Ephesus for having "tested those who say they are apostles and are not, and found them liars": these false apostles speak false words about themselves to deceive.
2. The lie can also qualify a thing, a word, or a testimony that does not conform to reality. Acts 6:13 reports that "false witnesses" testified against Stephen — their words were contrary to the facts.
3. More broadly, a liar is anything that contradicts truth or integrity. The Bible places lying among serious sins: in Revelation 21:8, "all liars" will inherit the lake of fire, alongside the cowardly and murderers, for lying corrupts the soul.
G5571.origine: The word comes from the verb "pseudomaï" (ψεύδομαι) which means "to deceive" or "to lie." It evokes the image of one who deliberately strays from the truth to mislead others. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, this word translates notably "sheqer" (שֶׁקֶר), which denotes lying and deception, and "shav" (שָׁוְא), the useless or vain, that which has no real substance.
G5571.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, exclusively in Acts and Revelation. In Acts 6:13, it qualifies the witnesses who accused Stephen of blasphemy — people of false words. In Revelation 2:2, Jesus commends the church of Ephesus for having discerned and rejected false apostles, that is, those who lie about their true spiritual identity. In Revelation 21:8, lying is at the heart of the sins that exclude from the Kingdom and condemn to hell. The emphasis is on voluntary and malicious lying: intentional deception, not a mere mistake.
G5571.portee: Lying is never trivial in the eyes of the Bible: it corrupts the relationship between humans and with God, who is himself truth. The Christian is called to cultivate sincerity and discernment: to discern false prophets and false apostles who deceive about their true spiritual nature. It is a warning about the importance of truth and integrity in the Christian life.

sens: Master or religious leader who teaches a doctrine contrary to Christian truth
Seductor who leads believers away from the authentic Gospel through deceptive teachings
G5572.detail:
1. A false teacher is a religious master who claims to teach in the name of God or Christ, but whose teaching is contrary to the true Gospel. Peter calls him "false" not because he lacks competence, but because he distorts the doctrine: these men "will introduce destructive sects" and deny the Master who bought them (2 Peter 2:1). He is a deceiver who presents himself as an authentic spiritual guide.
2. The false teacher acts as a seducer who disturbs faith. He does not openly teach error, but "introduces" destructive sects — separate groups founded on lies. In 2 Peter 2:1, Peter warns that these men bring sudden destruction upon themselves, for they deny Christ and lead others into their downfall.
G5572.origine: The Greek compound word combines "pseudos" (false, deceiver) and "didaskalos" (master, teacher, one who teaches). The image is that of a teacher who wears the garb of the authentic master, but whose word does not come from God. This term conveys the idea of a religious imposture: someone who deceives by presenting himself as what he is not.
G5572.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:1. Peter uses it to warn Christians against internal heresies that threaten the Church. He associates the false teacher with the false prophet, recalling Christ's warning about wolves coming "in sheep's clothing" (Matthew 7:15). Peter emphasizes that these seducers do not come from outside, but arise "among you," from within the Christian community, which increases the danger.
G5572.portee: Peter's warning remains relevant for every Christian. It teaches us not to passively believe every teacher who claims to be from God, but to examine the teaching in light of the Gospel. It reminds us that the greatest danger to faith often comes from those who speak the language of faith but have lost their attachment to the authentic Christ. It is an invitation to remain vigilant and rooted in the Word of God.

sens: One who utters lies, who speaks falsely
One who claims an authority that he does not have, especially in religious teaching
G5573.detail:
1. The word literally designates one who utters lies, who speaks falsely instead of telling the truth. It is a lie that comes from the mouth, a deliberately deceptive discourse. In 1 Timothy 4:2, Paul applies it to false teachers who teach prohibitions contrary to the word of God.
2. The meaning becomes clearer in its context: it is not just someone who occasionally lies, but one who consciously fabricates a lie to deceive and seduce. These false teachers present as true what is false, giving a religious authority to their deceptive teachings — hence the hypocrisy that Paul highlights.
G5573.origine: The Greek word combines two simple roots: "pseudès" (false, lying) and "logos" (word, discourse). It is a compound that describes one whose word is false by nature. The word "pseudès" comes from a root meaning to deceive or hide the truth. This type of compound was common in Greek to describe a permanent quality or state: it does not refer to an isolated false word, but to the character of one who speaks falsely.
G5573.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 4:2. Paul uses it to qualify the false teachers who arise in the last days, those who teach prohibitions regarding marriage and certain foods — human commandments presented as divine. The apostle emphasizes that these lies come from "false teachers" marked by a seared conscience. The context shows that it is a deliberate and systematic lie, not a sincere error, but a conscious deception serving a false teaching.
G5573.portee: This word warns the Christian reader to remain vigilant against those who confidently teach doctrines contrary to the Word of God. Paul is not speaking here of simple theological errors, but of voluntary lies, religious hypocrisy. Recognizing a "bearer of lies" helps the believer to test the spirits and not to be seduced by a false religious authority.

sens: to say things contrary to the truth to deceive
to deceive someone with lies
to falsely assert something in front of someone
to speak against the truth or fail to uphold the truth
G5574.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to utter a lie, to knowingly say what is false. It is to deceive by word. In Colossians 3:9, Paul exhorts Christians: "Do not lie to one another," for lying is incompatible with the new life in Christ.
2. The word can also mean to deceive someone in particular with lies. In Acts 5:4, Peter says to Ananias: "How could you have conceived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to men, but to God" — which shows that to lie is to target someone to deceive.
3. To lie also means to falsely assert something in communication: to speak ill falsely of someone (Matthew 5:11), or to deny communion with God while claiming to have it (1 John 1:6).
4. Lying stands in radical opposition to the nature of God and His word. In Hebrews 6:18, Scripture affirms "it is impossible for God to lie" — this is a fundamental principle: truthfulness is essential to God.
G5574.origine: The verb ψεύδομαι comes from the root ψεῦδος (pseûdos, the lie). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it generally translates כָּחַשׁ (kâchash), which means to deny, renounce, or be unfaithful to the truth. The Greek verb etymologically evokes the act of presenting a falsehood as a reality, to deceive by word. The family of words also includes the adjective "pseudès" (false) and the noun "pseudès" (liar).
G5574.emploi: The verb appears twelve times in the New Testament. Paul frequently uses it to solemnly affirm his sincerity: "I do not lie," he says in 2 Corinthians 11:31 and Galatians 1:20, calling God as witness. Acts shows it applied to the serious sin of Ananias and Sapphira, who lie by pretending to give the full price of their land to the Church (Acts 5:3-4). John uses it in a broader and spiritual sense: "If we say we have fellowship with Him and walk in darkness, we lie" (1 John 1:6), where lying means contradicting one's profession of faith by one's conduct. Hebrews 6:18 uses it to affirm the absolute impossibility that God lies — which undergirds the Christian's assurance.
G5574.portee: Lying is presented in the Bible as a serious sin that opposes the nature of God, who is absolute truth. For the Christian, this Word calls for radical honesty in word and deed: not to lie to others, but also not to lie to oneself about one's spiritual state. It also reminds us that God's absolute reliability — who cannot lie — is the foundation of all Christian hope.

sens: A person who gives false testimony in court
One who testifies against the truth
That which contradicts or denies reality
G5575.detail:
1. A false witness is someone who stands before a judge or authorities to assert things that are not true. It is an official lie, perjury. In Matthew 26:60, men present themselves as false witnesses against Jesus, seeking to obtain his condemnation through false testimony.
2. The term also extends to a figurative sense: to testify falsely or deceptively, to assert something that contradicts the facts. In 1 Corinthians 15:15, Paul states that the apostles would be false witnesses if they proclaimed the resurrection of Christ when it had not occurred — their testimony would be a claim contrary to reality.
G5575.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "pseudo" (false, lying) and "martyr" (witness, one who bears testimony). The term "martyr" comes from a root meaning to remember or be aware of something; a witness is therefore someone whose memory or conscience attests to a fact. By adding the prefix "false," it designates one whose testimony contradicts the truth.
G5575.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 26:60, during the trial of Jesus before the Sanhedrin, false witnesses are summoned to accuse Jesus, but their accusations are contradictory and invalid. In 1 Corinthians 15:15, Paul uses the term theologically: if the dead do not rise, then all who testify to the resurrection of Christ are false witnesses against God, for they assert something contrary to reality. In both cases, the word designates someone whose word has no value because it contradicts the facts.
G5575.portee: This word challenges Christians regarding the responsibility of testimony. Bearing witness to the resurrection of Christ is to affirm something crucial; if it were not true, those who proclaim it would entirely discredit themselves. Paul draws a certainty from this: since the apostles testified to the resurrection at the cost of their lives, they cannot be false witnesses — their message rests on an absolute truth. This invites every Christian to examine their own testimony: does it rest on a real encounter with Christ?

sens: To give false testimony in court
To assert against someone an accusation one knows to be false
To violate the divine commandment that forbids lying before the law
G5576.detail:
1. To bear false witness is to stand before a court and say things one knows to be false in order to condemn or accuse someone. It is judicial lying, a deliberately false accusation. When Jesus' enemies sought grounds to have him killed, "many bore false witness against him, but their testimonies did not agree" (Mark 14:56).
2. This term also designates the moral and spiritual infraction: violating the ninth commandment that forbids making false reports. Jesus enumerates the commandments for the rich young man: "You shall not bear false witness" (Matthew 19:18), placing it among the great sins like murder and adultery.
3. The imagery extends beyond the courtroom: it is to assert against someone something malicious that one knows to be false, with the intent to harm them. The infraction touches on fundamental honesty and justice.
G5576.origine: The Greek word combines "pseudos" (false, lying) and "martureuō" (to bear witness, to attest). It translates the Hebrew "anah" (Exodus 20:16, Deuteronomy 5:20), which literally means "to respond against" or "to speak against." The root evokes the idea of raising one's hand and speaking under oath — giving a public and solemn testimony. Adding "pseudo" (false) to this serious action makes it a grave violation of the trust placed in one who swears.
G5576.emploi: The verb appears mainly in the enumeration of the commandments (Matthew 19:18, Mark 10:19, Luke 18:20), where Jesus recalls the Mosaic Law to the rich young man. It reappears in the passion of Jesus (Mark 14:56-57), when false witnesses rise against him before the Sanhedrin — a moment when the ancient commandment against false testimony becomes a weapon against the Innocent himself. Saint Paul also cites it in Romans 13:9, recalling the commandments. The verb never designates a simple ordinary lie, but always a public lie, under oath, before a court or in a context of solemn accusation.
G5576.portee: This word reminds Christians that God values truth and justice. To bear false witness is not only to deceive but to destroy the trust upon which the community rests. It is also to betray the one against whom one lies, delivering them from innocence to condemnation — a grave sin that Scripture places on the same level as murder. For the disciple, this means that moral integrity, especially when one engages their word, is a non-negotiable requirement of God's Law.

sens: A false word reported in court to accuse someone
A deliberate lie used as a weapon against others
G5577.detail: 1. False testimony is primarily a false statement made before judicial authorities, with the aim of condemning an innocent person. In Matthew 26:59, the chief priests and the Sanhedrin seek a "false testimony" against Jesus, sufficient to have him killed: it is the weapon of those who want to dispose of someone by perverting justice. 2. More broadly, false testimony is any lie that one spreads against someone to harm or dishonor them. Jesus lists false testimony in Matthew 15:19 among the "evil thoughts" that "come from the heart" — he places it on the same level as murder and theft, for it is a sin that arises from within and destroys the life of others through words. It is a lie turned into a weapon.
G5577.origine: The Greek word combines "pseudo" (false, lying) and "marturia" (testimony, from "martus," one who bears witness). In Hebrew, false testimony is called "ʿēd šāqer" (literally "lying witness"). It is a sin severely condemned in the Law of Moses: Deuteronomy commands that the false witness be punished as they would have wished to harm the innocent.
G5577.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew. Jesus mentions it in Matthew 15:19 as a product of the evil heart — a thought that expresses itself in destructive words. A few chapters later, in Matthew 26:59, false testimony becomes the judicial instrument of those who want to eliminate Jesus. These two uses show that there is a continuity of sin: the inner lie manifests itself in public accusation, and the false witnesses in Jesus' trial illustrate exactly what Jesus has just denounced.
G5577.portee: False testimony reminds us that words are a formidable weapon and that we are accountable before God. For a Christian, this means keeping one's tongue from lying, not accusing others lightly, and refusing to participate in slander or unfounded accusations — even in favor of a cause that seems just. It is also a warning: he who lies against his neighbor lies against the truth itself.

sens: a person who claims to speak in the name of God but lies
a religious impostor who deceives the faithful with false predictions or false miracles
a figure of spiritual seduction and doctrinal danger
G5578.detail:
1. A false prophet is someone who claims to bring a word from God but deliberately lies or is mistaken. In Acts 13:6, Bar-Jesus is described as a "false Jewish prophet" — he is a religious impostor who assumes an authority he does not have.
2. These impostors seduce with deceptive appearances or spectacular miracles. Matthew 7:15 compares them to "ravenous wolves in sheep's clothing": they appear harmless on the surface, but they hide a destructive intent. Matthew 24:24 specifies that they perform "great signs and wonders" to mislead even the most solid believers.
3. The false prophet symbolizes a major spiritual danger: seduction and religious deception. Luke 6:26 warns that "all men" praise false prophets, while true prophets of God are hated — the world's approach is the opposite of God's.
G5578.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: "pseudo" (false, lying) and "prophetēs" (prophet, one who speaks in the name of God). The Hebrew נָבִיא (nabi) designates the authentic prophet who receives and proclaims the word of God. The Greek Scriptures of the Hebrew prophetic books (Zechariah, Jeremiah) use the same word for prophet, hence the interest in constructing its opposite to designate religious imposture.
G5578.emploi: The term appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly concentrated in the words of Jesus (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in the warnings of the apostles (Peter, John, Revelation). Jesus speaks of them in his eschatological discourses: in Matthew 24:11 and 24 and Mark 13:22, he announces their multiplication in the last days, alongside the appearance of false Christs. The emphasis is on their seductive ability ("will deceive many") and on the danger they pose to believers. In 1 John 4:1, John urges to "test the spirits" to distinguish true prophets from false ones. In 2 Peter 2:1, false prophets are associated with destructive heresies. In Revelation, they play a role as accomplices of eschatological lies (16:13, 19:20, 20:10).
G5578.portee: This word warns the believer against religious imitation: a message may seem pious, miraculous, appealing, without being from God. Jesus and the apostles therefore urge the disciple to exercise discernment, to know the true voice of God so as not to be seduced. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and to being rooted in the authentic Word of God.

sens: A word or statement contrary to the truth
Deliberate deception, the act of deceiving
An idol or false god worshiped instead of the true God
What is false, counterfeit, without foundation
G5579.detail:
1. A lie is primarily a word that contradicts the truth. This is what Jesus denounces in the devil: "When he lies, he speaks out of his own character; for he is a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44). The lie comes from the mouth of one who has no truth in him.
2. A lie is also a deliberate act of deception. It directly opposes the virtue of speaking the truth. Paul exhorts the Ephesians: "put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor" (Ephesians 4:25), as if lying were a habit to be abandoned.
3. A lie can also refer to what one worships in place of God: the pagans have "exchanged the truth about God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator" (Romans 1:25). To idolize is to believe a lie about who God is.
4. More broadly, a lie is anything that is false, counterfeit, lacking real foundation — like the "lying wonders" of 2 Thessalonians 2:9 which imitate authentic miracles but are an illusion meant to deceive.
G5579.origine: The Greek word pseudos comes from a root meaning "to deceive, to deviate from the truth." In Hebrew, the Bible mainly uses shéqer (lie) and kavasj (deception) to express this idea. The lie is presented from the Old Testament as the weapon of evil: it is through a lie that the serpent deceives Eve, and the Bible links the lie to the devil and to the distancing from God.
G5579.emploi: The word "lie" appears about ten times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles and Revelation. John connects it to the devil and the absence of truth (John 8:44, 1 John 2:21, 1 John 2:27). Paul opposes it to the truth that one must live as Christians (Romans 1:25, Ephesians 4:25) and describes the lies of the future impostor (2 Thessalonians 2:9, 2:11). Revelation shows that those who commit lies cannot enter the heavenly city (Revelation 21:27, 22:15), while God's elect are exempt from it (Revelation 14:5). The lie is always presented as incompatible with life in God and eternity with Him.
G5579.portee: For the believer, understanding that the lie is contrary to the truth of God must transform daily life: speaking the truth is not an option, but a requirement for those who follow Christ. Recognizing that the devil is the father of lies also helps discern how the adversary operates — through seduction and counterfeiting — and to guard against it. Finally, knowing that lies will have no place in eternity gives a real reason to cultivate honesty and sincerity right now.

sens: an impostor who claims to be the Messiah
a person who usurps the authority and titles of Christ
G5580.detail:
1. A false christ is someone who claims to be the Messiah promised by God, while he is not: he is an impostor, a usurper of the most sacred title. In Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22, Jesus warns his disciples that such false messiahs will arise, capable of performing impressive wonders to deceive even the elect — a serious warning against spiritual seduction.
2. The word also designates, more broadly, anyone who unduly arrogates the role, authority, or powers that belong solely to Christ: one who poses as a savior, a divine mediator, or a figure of ultimate spiritual authority, thus usurping the place that belongs to the true Messiah.
G5580.origine: The Greek word is composed of "pseudos" (false, lying) and "christos" (anointed, Messiah). It literally designates a false messiah, a counterfeit messiah. The word "christos" comes from the Hebrew "mashiah," which means "anointed" — one who has received divine anointing. By combining false + christ, the Greek isolates a category of religious seducers that was very real at the time of the New Testament.
G5580.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, in the two parallel passages where Jesus prophesies about the end times: Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22. In these two verses, Jesus places the false christ alongside the false prophet as a precursor sign of judgment. The emphasis is on the seductive nature of these impostors: they are not beggars or madmen, but figures credible enough to perform miracles and attract crowds. Jesus warns his disciples: true faith cannot rest on external miracles or rhetorical persuasion, but on the knowledge of the revealed truth.
G5580.portee: This word invites the Christian to spiritual vigilance. The Bible does not promise a world spared from religious seduction: on the contrary, it announces it. A false christ does not necessarily wear a grotesque mask — he can be impressive, miraculous, eloquent. True protection is not credulity towards every spectacular sign, but being rooted in the Word of God and knowing Christ himself, the only true Messiah.

sens: Who bears or gives a false name
Who presents themselves under a misleading or usurped name
Who falsely claims to be what they are not
G5581.detail:
1. The word describes someone or something that presents itself under a name that is not its own — a false name, a pseudonym, a counterfeit identity. In 1 Timothy 6:20, Paul warns Timothy against "science, falsely so-called," meaning against supposed knowledge that claims the title of "science" but does not deserve it: these are intellectual impostors, lying doctrines that usurp the prestige of true knowledge.
2. More broadly, the term applies to anything that presents itself under a false label: a false friend, false wisdom, false virtue. The lie resides not only in the name but in the contrast between the displayed appearance and the hidden reality.
3. Spiritually, the word emphasizes the danger of religious or intellectual imposture — when evil disguises itself as good, when error claims to be truth, when ideas contrary to faith adorn themselves with the prestige of science or wisdom.
G5581.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: ψευδής (pseud-, "false") and ὄνομα (onoma, "name"). It literally means "under a false name." The root ψευδ- evokes all forms of lying or deception, while onoma refers to the name one bears or gives to something. Together, they form the idea of something that presents itself under an usurped name, a false identity.
G5581.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:20. Paul instructs Timothy to "avoid profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science, falsely so-called." This is about keeping the faith pure in the face of heretical doctrines that claimed to be true "gnosis" (spiritual knowledge) but were merely dangerous impostures. The context suggests that these false doctrines — likely related to emerging Gnosticism — presented an intellectual prestige they did not deserve. The word thus critiques any false pretension: what displays an honorable title but whose content is corrupt.
G5581.portee: This word challenges the modern believer regarding their spiritual vigilance. It warns us that lies and heresy often disguise themselves as respectable wisdom or science, and that it is not enough to consider appearance or title to discern the truth. A lie wrapped in a beautiful name remains a lie. It invites us to examine the actual content of the doctrines presented to us, not just their displayed claims.

sens: a statement contrary to the truth
a deliberate deception
that which conceals or distorts reality
G5582.detail:
1. A lie is a word that contradicts the truth, a falsehood stated. In Romans 3:7, Paul refers to "my lie" to denote an accusation made against him: he is suspected of lying by claiming that God benefits from his sins, a serious falsehood aimed at discrediting him.
2. A lie involves an intention to deceive, to present the false as true. It is a deception of language, a distortion of speech to serve a personal or malicious interest.
3. By extension, a lie represents anything that conceals, distorts, or obscures the truth. It is a voluntary deviation from reality: a lie opposes the transparency and fundamental honesty that the Bible values.
G5582.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to deceive" or "to speak falsely." It denotes the act or concrete result of lying: the false word itself, the statement that deceives. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates Hebrew terms expressing falsehood and deception.
G5582.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 3:7. Paul uses it in a tight argument about the justice of God: he rejects the malicious accusation that he teaches one must do evil so that good may come. He calls this false imputation a "lie," which distorts his message and tarnishes his integrity. The context shows that the lie is a weapon of slander, an invented accusation meant to discredit a person and their teaching.
G5582.portee: This word reminds Christians that words carry serious spiritual weight: a lie is not a detail, but a rupture with the truth of God. By rejecting lies, even when they seem beneficial, we honor the God of truth and protect the clarity of the Christian testimony. Faithfulness to the truth is a mark of spiritual integrity.

sens: one who tells lies, who does not speak the truth
one who denies or refuses what is true
one who breaks promises or commitments
one who is mistaken about the nature of God or His word
G5583.detail:
1. A liar is someone who deliberately speaks falsehood, who does not stand in the truth. Jesus says of the devil that he "is a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44), it is his very nature to distort reality.

2. A "liar" is one who claims to know God but denies or contradicts Him through their words or actions. To say one has not sinned is to "make God a liar" (1 John 1:10) — one treats Him this way, accusing Him of not speaking the truth.

3. A liar is also one who breaks promises or claims to keep God's word without observing it: "Whoever says, 'I know Him,' but does not keep His commandments is a liar" (1 John 2:4).

4. The term applies to one who forges a false conception of God — claiming to love God while hating one's brother is to be a "liar" (1 John 4:20), for reality contradicts the lie.
G5583.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to deceive, to be mistaken, to speak falsely." In Hebrew, the Old Testament speaks of one who "lies" (כָּזַב, used to translate this Greek word in the Psalms and Proverbs). It is a simple word: it denotes the opposite of truth, the refusal or impossibility of remaining in reality. In the devil, lying is not an isolated act — it is his permanent nature, his fundamental character.
G5583.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the New Testament, almost always in the epistles of John and the writings of Paul. In the Gospel of John, it is used by Jesus Himself to describe the devil and his adversaries. Paul uses it to characterize those who oppose the truth: "liars" are ranked among serious sinners (1 Timothy 1:10). Remarkably, the word takes on a profound spiritual dimension: it is not just about a simple falsehood of speech, but a contradiction between what one says about God or oneself and reality. One who claims to know God or love Him without following Him is a "liar" — their life contradicts their words.
G5583.portee: This word challenges the believer: living in truth is much more than not lying — it means our lives must correspond to what we confess. If I say I know God or love Him, my actions must prove it; otherwise, I am a "liar." It is also a call to examine the influences around us: lies are not neutral; they come from the devil, the enemy of truth. Finally, this word reminds us that only God is absolutely true; every lie contradicts Him.

sens: To palpate, touch with the hands, feel by touch
To search by groping, to strive to find
To ascertain or verify by touch
To approach in a way that allows touching, to reach
G5584.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to palpate or touch something with the hands to have direct experience. In 1 John 1:1, the apostle John states that "our hands have touched" the word of life — this refers to the tangible and physical experience of having held the resurrected Jesus Christ. This is also the meaning in Luke 24:39, where Jesus invites his disciples to touch him to verify that he truly has a resurrected body: "See my hands and my feet... touch me and see." 
2. By extension, to touch means to search by groping, to strive to reach or find something in darkness or uncertainty. In Acts 17:27, Paul asserts that God wants the Gentiles to "seek him and perhaps feel their way toward him" — the image is that of a blind person searching hesitantly and laboriously. 
3. Touch can also simply mean to be able to reach or physically approach. In Hebrews 12:18, the text refers to "a mountain that can be touched" — it is a mountain accessible to touch, visible and tangible, in contrast to an invisible reality. 
4. In all these cases, the word emphasizes direct experience, personal and sensitive contact, rather than theory or abstract knowledge.
G5584.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that simply means "to touch" or "to palpate." It often translates the Hebrew terms mûsh and mashash, which evoke the action of touching, palpating, feeling with the fingertips. The root expresses the idea of direct and sensitive contact, which is also where its figurative use of searching, exploring, or experiencing comes from.
G5584.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in a context where direct and tangible experience is at stake. In Luke 24:39 and 1 John 1:1, it refers to touching the resurrected Jesus Christ — a motif of verification and reality of the glorified body. In Acts 17:27, the word shifts slightly in meaning: it describes the hesitant search for God by non-believers, an uncertain quest that proceeds by groping. In Hebrews 12:18, it qualifies the mountain of Sinai as something palpable and terrifying, contrasting it with the experience of the New Testament. The meaning thus oscillates between certain physical experience and laborious and uncertain searching.
G5584.portee: This word teaches us the importance of personal contact with God and His word. For the disciples, touching the resurrected Jesus was irrefutable proof of His reality and victory over death. For us, it reminds us that faith is not a distant abstraction, but a living and concrete experience. Even when we seek God "by groping," as Paul says to the Athenians, this sincere search is known to Him. The word invites us not to settle for purely theoretical knowledge, but to seek to meet Christ in a living and personal way.

sens: to count with pebbles or tokens
to evaluate a sum, expenses, a cost
to assess a number or its significance
to estimate, mentally reckon
G5585.detail:
1. In ancient Greek, the word comes from the word "pebble" (psêphos): calculations were made by arranging small pebbles or tokens on an abacus, a kind of columned board. This is the primary image: to count materially. 
2. By extension, it means to evaluate an expense or costs. In Luke 14:28, the one who wants to build a tower "calculates" the cost first to see if he has enough to finish. It is a practical and prudent calculation. 
3. The word also applies to assessing a number or interpreting its significance: in Revelation 13:18, the seer invites the one who has understanding to "calculate" the number of the beast (666), meaning to meditate on it and grasp its meaning.
G5585.origine: The word comes from the root "psêphos" (pebble, stone). Among the Greeks, pebbles or tokens were used for counting and voting: each person would cast a white or black pebble according to their choice. This is where the verb "to vote" in classical Greek comes from. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the often-used equivalent is the verb "sâfar" (to count, to recount), translated by this word in Greek in certain passages.
G5585.emploi: The verb "to calculate" appears only 2 times in the New Testament, in the two provided passages. In the Sermon on the Mount in parable, Jesus uses it to describe the prudence of the builder who evaluates his costs before building (Luke 14:28): it is a concrete and material calculation. In Revelation (13:18), John uses it to invite a calculation of spiritual interpretation, to "calculate" or decode the symbolic number 666. In these two contexts, the verb emphasizes the necessity of reflecting, evaluating, and understanding before acting or judging.
G5585.portee: This word reminds believers of the importance of practical wisdom and reflection. Building one's life or faith commitment requires discernment, like calculating real costs. It is also an invitation not to passively accept what one encounters, but to reflect, interpret, and seek deeper meaning — especially in the face of the spiritual enigmas of Revelation.

sens: Small smooth stone, pebble
Vote, suffrage (by metaphor: voting was done with pebbles)
G5586G.detail:
1. A white pebble: a small smooth and white stone. In Revelation, Jesus promises the victor a "white pebble" on which is written a new name that only the recipient knows (Revelation 2:17). This white stone likely symbolizes approval and honor, as a personal mark of authenticity and selection. 
2. A vote, a suffrage: among the Greeks, voting was done by casting pebbles into a urn — white for approval, black for rejection. Thus, the word "pebble" eventually came to designate the vote itself, although this usage does not explicitly appear in the passages provided here.
G5586G.origine: The word comes from a Greek root evoking the action of rubbing or polishing. This is why it primarily designates a small smooth stone, a pebble — polished by friction. In classical Greek, due to the practice of voting by pebbles (pebble voting), the word also came to mean a vote or judgment. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words for "stone" or "pebble."
G5586G.emploi: The word appears once in the New Testament, in Revelation 2:17, in the context of the promise made by Christ to the victors of the Church. It is symbolic: a "white pebble" bears a new secret name. The contrast between the whiteness of the pebble and the obscurity of the name (known only to God) emphasizes the intimacy and authenticity of the relationship between Jesus and the believer who triumphs.
G5586G.portee: This image of the white pebble reveals the personal tenderness of Jesus toward each child of God. It reminds us that spiritual victory is not a collective abstraction, but an individual reality, marked by a secret and intimate bond with the Lord. The believer who perseveres receives a personal confirmation of their identity in Christ, known only to God.

sens: small polished stone or pebble
vote expressed by placing a stone in a ballot box
right to vote or opinion in a decision
G5586H.detail:
1. In ancient Greece, a small smooth stone was used as a voting instrument: it was placed in a ballot box to express one's choice. This is the concrete image of the word "suffrage."
2. By extension, the word refers to the act of voting itself — the expression of an opinion by this means. In Revelation 2:17, the "white stone" is an allusion to this positive vote, a sign of favor or approval.
3. More generally, "suffrage" can mean the right to participate in a decision, or the opinion one contributes to it. Paul recalls in Acts 26:10 that he "gave his vote" with that of others to condemn Christians, meaning he approved and supported these death sentences.
G5586H.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to rub" or "to polish," as the stones used for voting had to be smooth. In Greek, the notion of stone is also found in the context of games or judgments. When the Greek Bible of the Old Testament encounters the Hebrew word צֹר (stone), it can express it with this same term, although here the context is specifically that of Greek democratic voting.
G5586H.emploi: This word is very rare in the New Testament: it appears only once in the attested uses, in Acts 26:10. There, Paul confesses that when he persecuted Christians, he "gave his vote" with the other judges or authorities to condemn them to death. The context is one of participation in a capital sentence. The word refers to the well-known Greek practice of voting by pebble, a practice also found in the Hellenized culture of the first century Middle East. The mention of the "white stone" in Revelation 2:17 plays on the same imagery: the white pebble, unlike the black or other colors, symbolized a favorable judgment.
G5586H.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the sins of its witnesses before their conversion. Paul openly acknowledges having participated in the condemnation of the disciples, giving his approval to their executions. For the Christian reader, this is a lesson in sincere repentance and the transformative grace of God, which changed a persecutor into an apostle. It is also an invitation to examine our own approvals and our silence in the face of injustices.

sens: malicious words whispered secretly against someone
defamation spoken softly or in the background
denigrating remarks spread discreetly
G5587.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a whisper, words spoken softly — but not just any words: these are malicious words, accusations against someone else. It is slander that occurs in the background, softly, like poison spread in the shadows. In 2 Corinthians 12:20, Paul lists the sins he fears he will find among the Corinthians: quarrels, jealousy, but also these "slanders" — these destructive whispers that undermine a community in silence.
2. Unlike an accusation made openly face to face, slander spreads furtively, from mouth to ear. It hurts because it spreads without the targeted person being able to defend themselves or hear the true reason for the hostility. It is a sin that reveals the heart of a man who does not dare to confront openly but prefers shadow and lies.
G5587.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb that literally means "to whisper" or "to murmur." This image of whispering captures the essence of the word: malice that spreads softly, never openly. The root evokes the idea of words that escape like a breath, discreetly disseminated in a corrosive manner.
G5587.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:20. Paul, anticipating his visit to Corinth, lists the shortcomings he fears: quarrels, jealousy, animosities, cabals, gossip, slander, and troubles. These slanders are among the symptoms of a spiritually sick community. They are the fruit of the flesh, not of the Spirit, and reveal a divided heart that prefers discreet destruction to honest edification.
G5587.portee: For the Christian, this word invites self-examination: do we speak about others in whispers or do we seek to resolve our differences face to face? Slanders may seem less serious than other sins because they are done in secret, but they are insidious — they erode trust and unity in the body of Christ. Fleeing slander means choosing light and truth over shadow and lies.

sens: one who speaks softly and in secret
one who spreads slander or gossip in hiding
one who intrigues with malicious insinuations
G5588.detail:
1. The word literally refers to one who murmurs, who speaks softly — this is the basic meaning of the verb from which it comes. Imagine someone whispering: this is the image of the word (in ancient Greek, it was even an epithet of the god Hermes, the divine messenger who spoke softly).

2. But the Bible uses this word in a pejorative sense: the one who murmurs is one who speaks in secret to slander, who spreads gossip, calumnies, and insinuations against someone else. It is the wicked one who destroys another's reputation by whispering in corners (Romans 1:29).

3. More broadly, it is one who intrigues, who sows discord through rumors and sly words, without having the courage to say things openly: a gossip.
G5588.origine: The word comes from the verb "psithyrizô" which means "to whisper, to murmur." The root naturally evokes the sound of murmuring, whispering — a soft but clandestine noise. In Greek, it was an epithet of Hermes, the messenger who speaks softly. But in a biblical context, this murmur becomes a weapon of malice: the one who murmurs speaks evil, in secret, to harm.
G5588.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Romans 1:29, where Paul lists the vices and sins of men who have turned away from God. Paul classifies it among "wickedness, greed, malice, envy, murder, strife, deceit" — all behaviors that destroy human relationships. The context shows that "the one who murmurs" is a sower of discord, someone whose sin consists of speaking in secret to harm others. It is a widespread vice, accompanying pride and a lack of fear of God.
G5588.portee: This word reminds us that small words, whispers, gossip, and slanders spoken "among us" are not small sins: it is an active form of malice. The Bible places the one who murmurs on the same level as the murderer or the envious. This invites us to monitor not only our open words but also the secret conversations, insinuations, and rumors we spread: it is a reflection of our heart.

sens: Fragment of bread or food that falls during a meal
Tiny portion, insignificant remainder
Figuratively: what remains when the essential is given to others
G5589.detail:
1. A crumb is a small piece of bread or food that naturally escapes from the table during a meal — a very concrete and everyday image. Jesus imagines the little dogs eating the crumbs that fall from the master's table (Matthew 15:27 and Mark 7:28).

2. The word also designates a derisory portion, a worthless remnant: poor Lazarus can only feed on the crumbs — these tiny scraps — that escape from the rich man's table (Luke 16:21). It is the very image of destitution.

3. Spiritually, the crumb represents a residual grace, a meager blessing given to one who has nothing — but even this crumb is enough for those who are hungry and humble.
G5589.origine: The Greek word ψιχίον is a diminutive (it diminishes, shrinks) of the word ψίξ, which means crumb or fragment. This diminutive adds to the idea of smallness a touch of affection or picturesque quality. The word paints the image of fragmented, scattered food, reduced to its smallest elements — which perfectly fits the small pieces falling under a table.
G5589.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in meal scenes that contrast the rich with the poor, the master with the servant. In Matthew and Mark, it illustrates the humility of the Syrophoenician woman who accepts the crumbs as grace, comparing her state to that of the little dogs. In Luke, it describes the misery of poor Lazarus, reduced to begging for the crumbs from the rich man's banquet. In all cases, the crumb symbolizes radical deprivation, but also confident hope.
G5589.portee: The crumb teaches two opposing lessons: the humility that knows how to receive little (the faith of the Syrophoenician woman) and the cruel indifference of the rich who refuse even the crumb to the poor (the rich man in Luke 16). For the believer, it reminds us that Christ never turns away anyone who comes to Him with humility, even if they consider themselves unworthy of more than a mere crumb.

sens: the vital breath that animates the body
the person, the individual, the living being
the seat of will, desires, and feelings
the object of God's eternal judgment and salvation
G5590G.detail:
1. The soul is primarily the breath of life that animates the body: it is what makes a creature live. When the soul leaves the body, it is death. In Matthew 10:28, Jesus speaks of one who can "kill the soul" — that is, annihilate life itself, not just the physical body.

2. By extension, the soul designates the person itself, the whole individual: saying "many souls were converted" (Acts 2:41, implicitly) means "many people." This is a Semitic way of speaking: instead of saying "the man" or "the person," one says "the soul."

3. The soul is also the home of inner life: will, love, deep feelings, desires. To love God "with all your soul" (Mark 12:30) means to love Him with all your being, with all your emotional strength. In 1 Peter 1:22, purifying your soul means transforming your heart and inclinations by obeying the truth.

4. Finally, the soul is the object that God cares about for eternal salvation. Hebrews 13:17 speaks of watching over souls — that is, over the spiritual well-being and eternal destiny of individuals. James 1:21 invites us to receive the Word that "can save your souls."
G5590G.origine: The Greek word ψυχή comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to breathe" or "to blow." It primarily designates the vital breath, life itself. In Hebrew, it mostly translates the word נֶפֶשׁ (néphesh), which has exactly the same meaning: the breath of life, but also the living person, and by extension, feelings and desires. Both Greeks and Hebrews viewed life not as an abstraction, but as something concrete: the breath, the principle that makes one move and act.
G5590G.emploi: The word appears 46 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Gospels and the letters of Peter. It primarily designates biological life (Matthew 10:28: the soul can be killed) or death (Acts 2:27: the soul remains in the realm of the dead). But it also takes on a much broader meaning: the whole person, with their affections and wills. To love God or one's neighbor "with all your soul" means to engage one's entire self. The letter to the Hebrews frequently uses the term for the object of eternal salvation: the soul that must be saved (Hebrews 10:39), the soul anchored in hope (Hebrews 6:19). In Revelation, the souls of the martyrs (Revelation 6:9) refer to the individuals themselves in their spiritual reality, judged and glorified.
G5590G.portee: This word reminds us that the human being is not reduced to their body: there is within them a spiritual, intimate, irreplaceable reality that God knows and cares for. To lose one's soul (Mark 8:37) means to lose the essential: not just one's life, but one's eternal future with God. It is a call not to sacrifice the lasting and the spiritual for temporal gains. For the believer, the soul is what God saves, protects, and transforms: that is why it must be nourished by the Word and obedience.

sens: The vital breath, life itself
What animates and gives life to the body
The seat of will, desires, and feelings
The person themselves, the individual
What is the object of God's eternal salvation
G5590H.detail:
1. The soul is primarily the breath of life, what makes one live. When the soul leaves the body, the person dies. This is the image of the original Hebrew word that literally means "breath." Matthew speaks of those who sought the "life" of the little child (Matthew 2:20): it is this vital force that is threatened.

2. What gives life to the body is called the soul. It cannot be seen, but without it, there is only a corpse. Jesus asks: "Is it lawful to save a person or to kill them?" (Mark 3:4) — He speaks of a living soul, a life to be protected.

3. The soul is the place where wills, desires, and feelings are formed. When we love someone "with all our soul," we do not just give our hands or words; we give all that we are. Jesus says: "I will give my life for you" (John 13:37), meaning His entire being, His limitless love.

4. The soul can simply refer to the person, the individual. When Revelation speaks of "three thousand souls" converting at Pentecost (Acts 2:41, although this verse is not in our precise references), it counts people. It is a Semitic way of saying "three thousand people."

5. The soul is finally what God wants to save for eternity. James says: "Whoever brings back a sinner from the error of their way will save a soul from death" (James 5:20) — not just earthly life, but eternal salvation.
G5590H.origine: The Greek word ψυχή (psuchē) comes from a root meaning "to blow" or "to breathe." It often translates the Hebrew word נֶפֶשׁ (néfesh) in the Greek Old Testament. In both Hebrew and Greek, the soul is what breathes, what animates, the principle of life. This is also why the word can refer to both physical life and the whole person with their feelings and choices.
G5590H.emploi: This word appears 34 times in the provided biblical references, especially in the Gospels and the Epistles. It is used in very different ways: 1) to speak of life that can be lost or saved, that is exposed to danger (John 13:37, Acts 20:24); 2) to describe the affections and desires of the heart, what one loves or wants (Matthew 6:25: "do not worry about your soul"); 3) to designate simply a person or individual, especially in the sense of eternal salvation (Luke 9:56: Jesus does not come to lose souls); 4) to speak of what one sacrifices or gives, as when the Good Shepherd lays down His life (John 10:11, 15). The meaning naturally shifts from the more concrete (the life one breathes) to the more spiritual (the eternal life one can receive or lose).
G5590H.portee: Understanding the soul as what God wants to save changes the perspective on life and death. It is not an abstraction: it is the whole being, inseparable from our feelings, our choices, our attachments. Jesus gives His life for our soul because He loves us, and the Father wants to save us entirely for eternity. It also reminds us that every soul matters to God — every person, even the most unworthy, is the object of His salvation.

sens: Life itself, the vital breath that animates the body
The seat of emotions, desires, and affections of the heart
The person itself, the individual considered in its essence
What in man can be saved or lost for eternity
G5590I.detail:
1. The soul is primarily life, the vital breath that makes living possible: it is the principle of life that animates the body. In Mark 14:34, Jesus says, "My soul is deeply grieved to the point of death," expressing a profound distress that affects his entire living being.

2. The soul also refers to the emotional and affective heart, the center of feelings: it is where sadness, joy, and desire arise. Luke 1:46 states, "My soul magnifies the Lord," where Mary expresses the exultation of her entire inner being. In John 12:27, Jesus says, "My soul is troubled," showing emotional turmoil.

3. The soul also signifies the person itself, the individual: it is a way of designating someone in their entirety. This is particularly common in passages translated from Semitic languages.

4. Finally, the soul is what can be saved or condemned, what exists beyond physical death and can be restored or lost eternally. In Hebrews 10:38 and 3 John 1:2, it represents the person in their spiritual destiny, the object of divine grace.
G5590I.origine: The Greek word psuchē comes from a root meaning "to breathe" or "to blow": it is the vital breath. In Hebrew, it primarily corresponds to nèfesh, which designates both physical life and the living person or soul. Both words share this image of the animating breath: the Hebrew nèfesh is primarily the throat or the gorge through which breath passes. The Greek psuchē has retained this original link with the idea of animated life.
G5590I.emploi: The word appears about 120 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Gospels and the Epistles. The provided usages show its multiplicity: it first designates the seat of emotions (Jesus in Gethsemane, Mary singing), then the whole person considered in their spiritual and moral dimension. A particularly important usage concerns the salvation or eternal perdition of the soul: it is what God can save (James 1:21), what is entrusted to His grace (1 Peter 1:9). Elsewhere, the expression "every soul" (Romans 13:1, Acts 2:43) simply means "each person." The word thus shifts from its most physical meaning (life, breath) to its most spiritual meaning (what endures eternally).
G5590I.portee: Understanding the soul as the seat of emotional and spiritual life helps the reader grasp that God cares about the whole being, including emotions and will, and not just external obedience. It is also an invitation to take eternal destiny seriously: the soul is not just a principle of life, but what can be saved or lost. For the believer, this means that their relationship with God engages their entire person, and that their faith affects the deepest part of their being.

sens: The vital breath, life itself
The inner self of a person: the heart, will, desires
A person, an individual
Eternal life, the object of divine salvation
G5590J.detail:
1. The soul is primarily the breath that animates a body, life itself — what makes a being live. This is the primary image of the word: the vital principle that one breathes.
2. The soul also designates the seat of inner life: what wants, desires, loves. In Romans 2:9, "every soul of man who does evil" speaks of the person in their moral interiority. It is the deep heart, the center of personality.
3. The soul becomes a simple way of saying "a person," "an individual." In Acts 2:41, "three thousand souls" are baptized — it is a Semitic way of counting people: each soul = each person. Similarly, in Romans 13:1, "let every person be subject" literally means "let every soul".
4. In the perspective of salvation, the soul is eternal life, what could be lost or saved, what God desires to save. This is the highest stake: the salvation of the soul is the blessed life with God.
G5590J.origine: The Greek word ψυχή comes from a root that means "to breathe" or "to blow." In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek often translates this word as נֶפֶשׁ (néfèsh), which has the same richness: first the vital breath, then the living person, then the inner life. This dual dimension — physical at first, then inner and personal — is at the heart of the word throughout the Bible.
G5590J.emploi: The word appears 9 times in these usages in the Segond 1910. It carries three main uses: first, counting people (Acts 2:41: "three thousand souls"), then speaking of the person or individual as responsible before God (Romans 2:9: the soul that does evil; Romans 13:1: every soul subject to authorities). Sometimes it simply designates the number of people: Acts 7:14 and 27:37 clearly show this with exact figures. The Segond 1910 translates according to the context: "soul" when the emphasis is on inner life or spiritual stakes, "person" when counting or enumerating individuals.
G5590J.portee: The soul reminds the Christian that they are not just a body: there is within them a depth, an inner life that matters infinitely more. Every person — oneself and others — is a soul that God desires to save. This word invites vigilance: every soul, including our own, is responsible before God and has eternal value. That is why caring for souls is so serious, and why God continually calls us to our inner life.

sens: The vital breath, life itself
The person in all their existence
The seat of feelings, desires, and will
The object of divine protection and salvation
G5590K.detail:
1. The soul is primarily the breath of life, what animates the body and makes it alive. This is the starting image: in Hebrew, the corresponding word (nephesh) literally means "breathing." When Jesus asks, "What will a man give in exchange for his soul?" (Mark 8:36), he speaks of life itself, what is most precious.
2. The soul designates the whole person, the individual being in their concrete existence. When Revelation says "every living soul" (Revelation 16:3), it means "every living being," "each creature." 
3. The soul is the center of emotions, wills, and affections: it is where love, desire, and decision arise. Jesus says, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your soul" (Mark 12:30): this means to love with all one's being, without reservation.
4. In biblical thought, the soul is also what God saves and protects for eternity. That is why James speaks of "saving a soul" (James 1:21, 5:20): it concerns the eternal salvation of the person.
G5590K.origine: The Greek word "psuchē" comes from a root that evokes breath and respiration. In Hebrew, it mostly translates "nephesh" (nefesh), which first designates the throat, then breathing, then life and the person. This same family is found in other Greek words like "psyche" (the heart of the living) and the French "psych-ique." The image is always the same: what gives life, what animates.
G5590K.emploi: The word appears very frequently in the New Testament, in all literary genres. It is first used in a concrete sense: physical life, particularly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) when speaking of giving or losing one's life. It then takes on a more spiritual significance: in Paul and Peter, the idea emerges that the soul is the stake of divine salvation. In Revelation 16:3, "every living soul" shows how the word can also simply mean "creature" or "being." Contexts of death, sacrifice, or salvation are particularly important: the soul is never a purely abstract reality, but always linked to the existence and destiny of the person.
G5590K.portee: Understanding the soul in the Bible means grasping that the human being is not an assembly of parts (body on one side, spirit on the other), but a living and indivisible person, fully concerned by God. This gives weight to our choices, our affections, our ordinary existence: all of this matters for eternity. It also teaches that Jesus gave his life (his soul) for our salvation — he gave himself entirely, without reserve.

sens: Pertaining to the natural soul, the physical world, and not to the Spirit
Governed by instincts and carnal desires rather than by faith
Earthly and contrary to divine wisdom
G5591.detail:
1. The "animal" man is one whose nature pertains solely to the natural soul, without access to the Spirit of God: he does not understand spiritual things because he judges them according to the world (1 Corinthians 2:14). It is like a body that would resurrect without transformation, remaining simply physical (1 Corinthians 15:44).
2. This "animal" nature opposes the spiritual nature: it is what comes first in man, what is simply alive but devoid of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:46).
3. A "carnal" wisdom that comes from below is "animal" because it is born of the earth, of the human heart left to itself, and it opposes the wisdom that comes from above (James 3:15).
4. "Sensual" men are those who cause divisions and lack the Spirit of God, governed by their passions rather than by faith (Jude 1:19).
G5591.origine: The word comes from the Greek "psychē" (ψυχή), which designates the soul or natural life. An "animal" man is literally a man governed by his psyche, his soul life, without the transformation of the Spirit. This distinction between the natural soul and the new spirit is characteristic of Pauline theology: the soul without the Spirit remains attached to earthly and carnal realities.
G5591.emploi: Paul uses this word five times in the New Testament to describe what belongs to the human nature untransformed by God. In 1 Corinthians 2:14, it refers to the unbeliever who cannot receive spiritual things. In 1 Corinthians 15:44-46, Paul applies it to the resurrected body of carnal men, before the transformation into a spiritual body. James 3:15 speaks of a "carnal" wisdom that comes from the earth rather than from heaven. In Jude 1:19, it refers to the "sensual" false teachers who divide the assembly. The word systematically designates what is surrendered to human nature without the transforming action of the Holy Spirit.
G5591.portee: This word invites the Christian to discern two levels of reality: what pertains to his natural life and what pertains to the action of the Spirit within him. It calls to reject a wisdom that would claim to come from God but remains attached to carnal desires and human reasoning. Recognizing the "animal" nature of what surrounds or tempts us is to choose to seek the wisdom from above and to remain under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

sens: Low temperature of the air or environment
Physical sensation of cold felt by the body
Trial or suffering related to difficult conditions
G5592.detail:
1. Cold refers to low temperature, this atmospheric or climatic state where it freezes. In John 18:18, the servants light a fire "because it was cold" — the word simply describes the climate of that winter night in Jerusalem.
2. Cold is also the sensation that the body feels in response to the atmospheric cold: this discomfort, this need to warm up. Paul's companions in Malta warm themselves by the fire in Acts 28:2 precisely because "it was very cold" — we see the immediate reaction of the body that suffers.
3. In its figurative or extended sense, cold becomes a physical trial, an element of suffering and deprivation: Paul enumerates in 2 Corinthians 11:27 all the evils he has endured "in cold and nakedness," alongside hunger, sleeplessness, and beatings — the cold is a true tribulation he has suffered.
G5592.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ψύχ- (psych-), which evokes cooling or the act of cooling. In Hebrew, there are similar terms (קֹר qor, קָרָה qarah) that mean cold or coolness. The Greek word ψῦχος is a neuter noun that concretely designates low temperature and its effects, without metaphorical ambiguity at its origin.
G5592.emploi: The word ψῦχος appears three times in the New Testament, always in the concrete sense of physical cold. John 18:18 mentions it during the scene where Peter warms himself by the fire in the courtyard of the Sanhedrin — the context suggests a cold winter night in Palestine. In Acts 28:2, Paul and his companions are exposed to it during the shipwreck in Malta, and the inhabitants help them by welcoming them by a large fire. In 2 Corinthians 11:27, Paul summarizes the apostolic sufferings he has faced, and cold is among the deprivations he endured during his missionary journeys. In all cases, the word remains attached to the physical and concrete experience of cold.
G5592.portee: For the Christian reader, this simple word reminds us of the reality of the body and the physical world in which God places us. Seeing Peter sitting by the fire in the cold helps to understand his state of mind during his denial — human vulnerability in the face of material trials. Paul's enumeration in 2 Corinthians 11 shows that following Christ requires accepting real bodily sufferings, not sought but endured with courage.

sens: Having a low temperature, cooling
Lacking warmth, fervor, commitment
G5593.detail:
1. The word literally designates what has a low temperature. In Matthew 10:42, Jesus speaks of a "cold glass of water": it is cooled water, pleasant to drink, in contrast to lukewarm or hot water. The image is concrete and simple.
2. Figuratively, the word applies to the spiritual attitude of a person or a church. In Revelation 3:15-16, Jesus reproaches the church of Laodicea for being "lukewarm" — neither truly cold nor hot. Here, "cold" would evoke indifference or spiritual coldness, an absence of passion for God. The contrast with "hot" (which means fervent, enthusiastic) shows that "cold" represents a lack of commitment or zeal in faith.
G5593.origine: The Greek word psuchros comes from the root psuchô (to cool, to blow cold wind). It first describes a physical sensation: what cools, what is cold to the touch. This root evokes the idea of cold wind or penetrating cold. The figurative use to describe a cold or indifferent spiritual attitude is natural: just as physical cold contrasts with warmth, a cold soul contrasts with a soul burning with zeal for God.
G5593.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the New Testament. In Matthew 10:42, it qualifies the water in a concrete and generous context: offering a simple glass of cold water to a disciple of Jesus. In Revelation 3:15-16, it takes on a spiritual and critical meaning: Jesus asks the church of Laodicea to be "cold" rather than lukewarm, which reveals the condemnation of moral and religious lukewarmness. The passage shows that Jesus would prefer a frank opposition (being cold or hot) to a lackadaisical indifference (being lukewarm). This is a reprise of the figurative meaning: the absence of zeal or commitment.
G5593.portee: For the Christian, this word invites self-examination: am I fervent or lukewarm in my faith? The mention of the "cold glass of water" also reminds us that even simple and practical gestures, motivated by love for Christ, have eternal value. The passage about Laodicea warns against spiritual complacency: God prefers a living and conscious faith, even if imperfect, to a religious appearance without depth.

sens: To become cool or cold, to lose heat
To lose vigor, intensity, or momentum (figuratively)
To diminish, decrease in strength or fervor
G5594.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word means to literally become cool or cold, to lose the heat one had. It is the image of a temperature dropping, like a hot drink cooling down.
2. In the figurative sense, which Jesus uses in Matthew 24:12, "to grow cold" refers to a loss of spiritual and moral intensity: love, charity, and the fervor of the heart diminish and weaken. Jesus announces that "the love of many will grow cold" — as if this burning love is gradually extinguished as iniquity increases around.
G5594.origine: The verb comes from the ancient Greek meaning "to breathe" or "to blow," a primary image of a breeze that cools. The word has naturally evolved to describe the action of becoming cool or cold. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses related roots (קוּר, שָׁטַח) when speaking of cooling or spreading; here Jesus takes up this image of lost warmth to evoke spiritual lukewarmness.
G5594.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 24:12. Jesus uses it in His discourse on the signs of the end times to describe the spiritual state of the world before His return. The love of believers, once burning, will grow cold due to the increase of sin and iniquity. It is a passive verb ("will grow cold"), emphasizing that this cooling happens not by a voluntary act, but as a natural consequence of the moral corruption that spreads.
G5594.portee: This word invites the reader to remain vigilant about the state of their own heart. Love for God and for others must not grow cold, even when evil seems to triumph around them. Jesus warns us: it is easy for our zeal to be extinguished in the face of the seductions and challenges of the world. It is a call to constantly revive our spiritual fervor and not to let indifference take hold of us.

sens: To give food, to nourish someone
To distribute food to others
To generously provide for material needs
G5595.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to give food to someone, as one feeds a child or a sick person by presenting food in small pieces. This is what Paul asks in Romans 12:20: "If your enemy is hungry, feed him" — an act of generosity towards one who suffers from hunger.
2. The word can also mean "to distribute food" in a broad sense, sharing provisions with those in need. In 1 Corinthians 13:3, Paul speaks of one who "would distribute all his goods for the food of the poor": the verb here denotes the action of giving one's food and resources to others.
3. Finally, the word can extend to the figurative sense of "providing for the vital needs" of someone, supplying their sustenance. It is an act of practical kindness, of responsibility towards one who depends on our help.
G5595.origine: The verb comes from the Greek noun ψωμός (a piece of bread, a morsel), which evokes the image of breaking food to give it. It is a relatively rare and late verb, used to describe the concrete act of feeding, particularly that of someone who is weak or dependent. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb meaning "to eat" in the active form, but applied to the one who gives or shares.
G5595.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 12:20, Paul uses it to urge believers to feed their hungry enemy — it is a concrete commandment of love for one's neighbor inspired by Proverbs. In 1 Corinthians 13:3, the same verb describes the action of distributing all one's goods for the food of the poor: Paul uses it to show that even extreme material generosity, without love, remains devoid of spiritual meaning. In both cases, the word denotes a concrete, visible act of sharing resources.
G5595.portee: This verb reminds us that the Christian faith is not limited to thoughts or feelings: it must be expressed in practical gestures of assistance and generosity. Feeding the hungry, sharing what one possesses, is to imitate the love of Christ and respond to the real needs of one's neighbor. Paul uses this word to show that brotherly love must produce concrete acts — and that this is the true measure of our faith.

sens: A small piece or fragment of food, particularly bread
What is given or shared at the table
What marks a relationship between the giver and the receiver
G5596.detail:
1. The word denotes a small piece, a morsel, especially of bread or food. It fits well with the gestures of a meal: Jesus dips the morsel in the dish and hands it (John 13:26).
2. It is an object of sharing at the table, the simple act of one who eats together. This should seal the friendship and communion between Jesus and the one who receives it.
3. In the context of John 13, this morsel becomes the sign of a sealed fate: as soon as it is given, Satan enters into Judas (John 13:27), and Judas hastens to leave (John 13:30). The morsel marks the moment when betrayal shifts from intention to act.
G5596.origine: The word comes from the Greek psōmós (piece, morsel) with a diminutive that emphasizes smallness. In Greek, diminutives can express affection or intimacy of the gesture. This term translates the Hebrew pittat (a piece torn or detached), which itself evokes the idea of sharing.
G5596.emploi: The word appears three times, all in John 13:26-30, at the heart of Jesus' last meal. It recurs at each stage of the drama: the preparation of the dipped morsel (verse 26), the moment when Satan acts (verse 27), and the flight of the traitor who holds it in hand (verse 30). John uses this humble food gesture to show how the intimacy of the meal shifts into betrayal.
G5596.portee: This morsel of bread illustrates a troubling truth: the closest communion can coexist with the most hostile intention. It is a reminder that sharing the table of Jesus requires sincerity of heart. For the reader, this highlights the gravity of betrayal — not as a violent act, but as a gesture of rupture in the simplest intimacy.

sens: To rub or grind between the hands
To glean or detach the grains from an ear
To prepare the grains by rubbing them to eat
G5597.detail:
1. The word describes the action of rubbing something between the hands or fingers to transform it. In Luke 6:1, Jesus' disciples, while passing through a grain field on the Sabbath, plucked heads of grain and rubbed them in their hands: that is, they rubbed them to separate the grains from their husks so they could eat them raw.

2. Rubbing is a practical manipulation: by rubbing the ears of grain, one releases the edible grains from the straw surrounding them. It is a simple, useful gesture, that of someone who is hungry and prepares their food on the go while walking through the fields.

3. This is not an act of malicious destruction, but a necessary preparation for nourishment. However, the Pharisees who saw this scene viewed it as a violation of the Sabbath rest, since even this form of work was prohibited on the Sabbath.
G5597.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to rub" or "to grind." It is related to close forms that all express gestures of rubbing or grinding. The starting image is manual and concrete: that of hands working a material to extract what is useful.
G5597.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 6:1. This occurrence is famous: it recounts how the disciples, hungry, picked heads of grain and rubbed them to eat the grains. The evangelist chooses this simple and vivid verb to show the exact gesture of the disciples, transforming the raw ears into food. It is a concrete detail that brings the scene to life and, above all, serves to introduce an important controversy with the religious authorities.
G5597.portee: This passage invites reflection on the Sabbath and God's mercy: Jesus will defend His disciples by reminding that the law of the Sabbath does not take precedence over human needs. It is a moment where the Gospel shows that Jesus values compassion and life more than ritual rules. For the reader, this simple gesture of rubbing becomes a symbol of the freedom that Jesus brings.

sens: the twenty-fourth and last letter of the Greek alphabet
the number 800 (when used as numerals)
symbol of what is final, of accomplishment
divine designation of Christ as the end of all things
G5598.detail:
1. Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, just as alpha is the first. It is simply the name of this letter in its alphabetical order.
2. In ancient Greek, letters also serve as numbers: omega is worth 800. This numerical function is purely practical, with no connection to the rest of the passage.
3. By its nature as the last letter, omega naturally becomes a symbol of what is final, last, accomplished. This figurative meaning is explicit in Revelation.
4. Jesus presents himself three times saying, "I am the alpha and the omega": he affirms that he encompasses everything, from the beginning to the end (Revelation 1:8, 21:6, 22:13). He is the starting point and the endpoint of all things, the one in whom everything is accomplished.
G5598.origine: The word omega comes from the Greek omega, literally "great o" (ô mega), because it is a major letter compared to sigma. It is borrowed from the Phoenician alphabet, from which the names of Greek letters also derive. The word alpha (the first letter) symmetrically corresponds to it. In Revelation, these two letters form a symbolic pair to denote totality: from the first to the last, from A to Z according to our modern expression.
G5598.emploi: The word omega appears only four times in the New Testament, all in Revelation. In 1:8, God Almighty declares himself to be the alpha and the omega; in 1:11 (according to some manuscripts), Jesus uses the same formula; in 21:6, the one who sits on the throne (God) reiterates this affirmation; in 22:13, Jesus himself concludes the book by appropriating it. Omega thus always refers to totality, eternity, the final accomplishment of God's will. It is a word of victory and fullness.
G5598.portee: This designation of Christ as alpha and omega is a profound word for the believer. It says that Jesus is not just a figure of the past, nor a distant promise: he is the one who masters the entire course of history, from beginning to end, and he is its ultimate fulfillment. It offers consolation: whatever happens, the beginning and the end are assured in Christ. It also calls for faith and hope in his glorious return.

sens: Particle of apostrophe to address someone
Expression of astonishment or surprise
Mark of reproach or blame
Exclamation of admiration or wonder
G5599.detail:
1. The particle oh is primarily a simple mark of address, a solemn way of calling someone by name. It places the person being addressed at the center of attention and gives weight to what is about to be said. Jesus uses it to address the Canaanite woman (Matthew 15:28) or to speak to his disciples (Acts 1:1).
2. It also expresses astonishment or surprise at an event, statement, or mystery. In Romans 11:33, Paul uses it while contemplating the unsearchable riches of God: "Oh, the depth of the riches!".
3. When it accompanies a word of reproach, oh reinforces the blame and indignation. Jesus says, "Oh, faithless generation" (Mark 9:19) to express his irritation at the lack of faith. Paul also uses it to deliver sharp rebukes (Acts 13:10).
4. It can mark admiration or wonder at something great or beautiful. The particle adds solemnity and emphasis, transforming a simple statement into a memorable exclamation.
G5599.origine: The particle oh comes from ancient Greek and has been used since classical times to call someone or to express a strong emotion. It is always addressed to someone named (a vocative in grammar). It is a purely interjective particle: it has no proper meaning, it is merely an emotional color added to speech. It is very frequent in Greek literature, and orators used it to capture the attention of their audience.
G5599.emploi: This particle is used 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in direct speeches. It appears primarily when someone forcefully or emotionally addresses someone else. Jesus uses it when he speaks to his disciples with reproach (Mark 9:19: "Oh, faithless generation"), when he expresses his admiration (Matthew 15:28: "Oh woman," in response to her great faith), or when he speaks solemnly (Luke 24:25). Paul uses it to address reproaches to the magician Elymas (Acts 13:10) or to solemnly address King Agrippa (Acts 26:3, implicit). Its usage varies little: it is always a mark of emphasis and emotion.
G5599.portee: This small particle reminds us that speaking to others is never neutral. When Jesus or Paul use oh, they do not speak detachedly, but engage their heart and authority. It invites the reader to recognize the moments when God or his messengers address us with urgency or tenderness, and to pay attention to the tone of what is being said. It is an invitation to truly listen, not just to hear.
